Telly Arnold founded TLA Group LLC, a Houston-based carrier that has run non-CDL box trucks for about three years. In that time the company has rented a truck, co-owned one, financed its own, hauled final-mile appliance deliveries and moved over the road. Her advice to new owners, drawn from each of those stops, comes down to two habits: know every line item behind your cost per mile, and change course quickly when a business model stops paying.
She came to trucking with a bachelor’s degree in accounting, a master’s degree in business and more than 20 years in corporate America. She is also a small business trainer at the University of Houston Small Business Development Center . She runs StraightConnect, a platform aimed at new box truck owners, and co-hosts a podcast , “The Box Truck Hustle,” with Sharif Brooks.
Arnold started TLA Group to create opportunities for her son, and she planned to run it alongside a full-time job. Her business partner, Sharif Brooks, who has more than 20 years in trucking and a CDL, would drive.
“I thought it was something easy I could do while I work full-time and that you can make a lot of money,” Arnold said in an interview with FreightWaves. “I kind of just watched what he did and I saw his work ethic and I was like, I got a driver. I got the business sense. Let’s start a trucking business.”
Three tries at a truck and the bills that followed
Getting a truck on the road took three tries, and the first was a rental. “We heard that you can rent a truck and then you don’t really have the commitment, but you do not know about how much it costs to rent a truck,” Arnold said.
A 50-50 ownership split on a truck with another party came next. “That was a disaster,” she said. The third try was a financed truck of its own, and a truck note came with it.
The biggest surprise was the expenses, and they started the day the company’s motor carrier authority went active. The first insurance deposit ran $4,000 to $5,000 against a monthly premium of about $2500. “That was alarming,” Arnold said. “Was not expecting that whatsoever.”
Then came renewal. “Also, finding out that even though you renew your insurance, that big deposit does not go away,” she said. “I didn’t realize that every time you renew your commercial policy, you’re having to pay a deposit every single time.”
The largest bill she named was a repair. The company’s first major mechanical breakdown cost about $10,000. Of everything on her list, including the deposit and the truck note, the repair bills are the ones she singles out.
“The mechanical bills — not maintenance, the mechanical bills,” she said. “When your truck breaks down, how expensive that is.”
Final-mile lessons
Finding freight came next, and the load board turned out to be the easy part. “People say when your MC becomes active, you can immediately start booking loads on the load board. That is very true. However, there’s not a lot of brokers that like to work with new authority,” Arnold said.
TLA Group sat for a month before it went looking for white-glove work, the appliance and furniture deliveries that new box truck owners are told pay $5,000 to $6,000 a week. “That’s not true,” she said. The company landed local carrier work first, then moved into appliance delivery after Hurricane Beryl made landfall in Texas in July 2024 . That is where it learned what claims cost.
“People tell you about the claims, but they don’t really go into deep details about the claims and how do you survive the claims and what can you do to prevent the claims so your check is not being pinched away,” Arnold said.
Her rule for anyone doing that work is documentation at every handoff: a photo of every side of the box at the warehouse, another once it is on the truck and another at the customer’s house, because damage can be concealed inside the packaging. TLA Group learned that on its first day.
“We were new. We didn’t know. We didn’t take pictures,” she said. “And so if you don’t have the pictures to support that this refrigerator, as an example, was damaged before we even did anything, you’re going to get hit with a claim. There’s no ifs or buts about it.”
Customer surveys carried their own risk. On one install, a stove scratched the inside of a customer’s door. Because the crew worked as contractors, TLA Group was responsible for the damage, and Arnold moved fast to keep a claim off the company’s insurance.
“I called a contractor within 24 hours to go out there, repair it, exact paint. I called him, I followed up, I did all the steps, great customer service, and he did a horrible survey on us,” she said. “And because he did a horrible survey on us, I didn’t get a route the next day.”
Over the road, from a phone
TLA Group left appliance delivery for over-the-road freight in February 2025. “We learned that we have to pivot really fast because when you sit in something too long and you’re seeing that is not a good business model for you, it’s best to make those changes quick instead of just drowning,” Arnold said.
Over the road works much the same for a box truck as for a semi, she said. The carrier searches a load board and decides how far out it will run, 500 miles or 1,000. Out of Houston, TLA Group prefers freight headed to the Midwest, where the truck bounces between loads. A load booked on Friday may deliver on Monday.
“We’re booking loads off the load boards like Truckstop, DAT. We have to have a pallet jack, straps. Sometimes we got to have PPE. It just really depends what’s on the load board at that time,” she said.
Her partner drove the first truck, and he drives the only truck TLA Group runs today. In between, when the company added a second truck, it hired drivers and kept one truck local. “Hiring drivers was another obstacle that I did not see, which is hiring drivers who are qualified to drive non-CDL because the box truck you don’t need a CDL, but you need that CDL knowledge, hours of service , post-trip, pre-trip, making sure you strap down the freight so we don’t get any type of claims,” Arnold said.
The company dispatches its own loads, and Arnold is moving into AI dispatch tools to shorten the search. She uses two: Truckstop’s AVA, a voice assistant the load board launched in July , and FleetWorks, which builds AI dispatch agents .
“Like on Truckstop, they have a tool called AVA where you could talk to AVA and tell her what you’re looking for,” she said. “And then there’s another company called FleetWorks that they’ll email us and say, ‘Hey, where are you looking? Where’s your truck at?’ And then we’ll tell them how much we can hold, what region we like to go.”
“What I like now is everything I do is on my phone,” Arnold said. “Book a load, factor it, everything is on my phone. I generally rarely have to go to my computer.”
Knowing the numbers
Arnold recently sat down with someone to go through every expense TLA Group carries. She already knew her cost per mile. Now she is learning what each line item inside it pays for.
“So when you’re negotiating, you’re knowing that if your rate per mile is $2 a mile, this is covering everything that is helping your truck to stay operational,” she said.
Fuel is the line that swings. “If the fuel fluctuates, it is going to hit you, but you still need to know your numbers,” Arnold said. TLA Group splits its fueling between two cards because one drafts its account on Friday and the other on Tuesday, and both carry discounts.
“All I can say is we’ve been used to struggling already, so we just come up with a game plan,” she said.
Cost-per-mile math also decides when to add a truck. Arnold would not put a second truck on a very young authority unless overhead stopped at insurance, fuel, driver pay and a dispatcher. Before an owner scales, she wants a bookkeeper keeping clean books and reports the owner can read.
“Before you jump into that second truck, know your numbers. It’s very important for you to know your numbers,” she said.
Drivers shape the insurance bill too. Safety violations affect it, she said, and turnover can make a small carrier look risky. “When I went from one truck to two trucks, drivers in and out, in and out, in and out, you look kind of high risk,” Arnold said.
After a year of stability with her partner driving, the company’s latest renewal came in “a lot better,” though Arnold is not sure the stability was why. “Maybe we’ll see next year,” she said. “It may go up three times the amount.”
A second truck is on the plan for 2027 or 2028. “I think we’re ready to scale. Our MC is aged. We built a good reputation,” Arnold said.
The numbers are where Arnold parts ways with the advice new owners find online. “There are a lot of social media gurus who are out here selling people pipe dreams,” she said. “They concentrate on revenue but you can make six figures in revenue and you need to look at your bottom line.”
She built StraightConnect in response. The platform features verified industry voices, and her podcast brings on dispatchers, box truck carriers and factoring companies to explain what to expect. Being in the industry taught her that trucking “is more than just moving freight,” she said.
“People are really out here struggling for information and you don’t know who’s really trying to just sell you a course or if they’re really just trying to help you,” Arnold said. “This is why I created my podcast and also why I created the platform StraightConnect because I looked for it and never could find it.”

By Alison Koo
19 October 2026
CMA CGM’s decision to be an early mover in LNG bunkering, amid the decarbonisation push, has paid dividends, according to the French carrier’s VP for bunkering and energy transition, Farid Trad.
At last week’s Singapore International Bunkering Conference and Exhibition (SIBCON), he recalled that In 2017, CMA CGM signed the first of a few 10-year agreements under which compatriot energy major TotalEnergies supplied 300,000 tons of LNG annually to the carrier in Rotterdam.
Deliveries commenced in 2020, using an LNG bunkering vessel commissioned by Mitsui OSK Lines for long-term charter to TotalEnergies.
Mr Trad said: “When you look at what is happening 10 years later, you can’t help but say what we have achieved is enormous. We went through the Ukraine crisis in 2022 after Covid, and now we have another geopolitical event in the Middle East. What’s certain is that any future strategy will be a combination of security of supply, decarbonisation, and competitiveness. Finding the holy grail will be around those three dimensions.”
In July 2025, CMA CGM and TotalEnergies announced a new 50:50 joint-venture for LNG bunkering logistics in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region, expanding their long-term cooperation and scaling supply up to 360,000 tons annually through 2040.
In conjunction with SIBCON, CMA CGM announced it would work with Singapore LNG Corp, which operates the LNG terminals, and the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, to develop liquefied bio-methane as a marine fuel at the world’s largest bunkering port by sales volumes.
By going upstream and operating its own LNG bunkering barges, Mr Trad said, the French shipping line was assured of fuel for its LNG dual-fuelled ships.
CMA CGM, the third-largest shipping line with a fleet of nearly 4.5m teu, has 157 containerships of 1.6m teu on order, all to run on LNG dual-fuel.
Explaining CMA CGM’s choice of LNG, Mr Trad said the gas reduced health hazards due to lower sulphur oxide and nitrogen oxide emissions.
Alluding to uncertainty in environmental regulations, he added: “To invest in the long run, we need some certainty on regulation, which is lacking today. Discussions are still ongoing at IMO. We are still waiting to see how it will all fit together.
“When we order a ship, we order it for 25 years. So we always need to have a longer view on where we’re standing and you have to go through different crises, ups and downs, [fuel] prices could be up, prices could be down.”
He said CMA CGM saw agility and pre-deployment as key success factors, given the repeated supply chain shocks since 2020.
“The key critical point is not the potential demand, but the ability of the network of LNG bunker barges to be wherever we require them in terms of agility.
“One of the key things is that redeployment and agility is one of the key factors to managing the container shipping fleet. So we need to be able to change trading patterns as quickly as possible. And for that, we need bunker barges to be available in all ports when we possibly need them. Not only in huge bunker hubs like Rotterdam, Shanghai, and Singapore, but there are other ports that are either secondary or less important.”

AbbVie’s next-gen dual-targeting therapy elicited higher rates of remission than its IL-23 inhibitor Skyrizi in a Phase 2a trial of Crohn’s disease, leading analysts to wonder if the blockbuster can be outdone.
AbbVie’s Skyrizi exceeded $10 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026—but when it comes to treating Crohn’s disease, the Chicago-based company is already looking for the next best thing. AbbVie reported Monday that a next-gen combo for the autoimmune disease beat the blockbuster biologic in a mid-stage study.
In the Phase 2a TARGET-CD study, ABBV-466—a combination therapy comprising the IL-23–inhibiting Skyrizi and an anti-α4β7 integrin antibody called trosunilimab—elicited higher rates of endoscopic remission than either part of the combo as a monotherapy, meeting the trial’s primary endpoint, AbbVie revealed in a press release . The result led BMO Capital Markets to ask: “Sky is the limit?”
“Early UEG data for ABBV-466 could chart a path for a more efficacious dual-targeting version of Skyrizi,” BMO analysts said in a note to investors Monday morning.
RBC Capital Markets analysts were similarly upbeat on the results, saying Monday that the trial delivers on the next-gen combination and “next leg” of AbbVie’s growth story.
“We see this as a win for ABBV’s lifecycle management with Skyrizi and for its next-gen agents in development, and reinforces our thesis that ABBV is building a durable moat in IBD through next-gen combo strategies,” the firm’s analysts wrote.
TARGET-CD randomized 300 patients 1:1:1 to ABBV-466, Skyrizi or trosunilimab for 24 weeks. At week 12, 30.2% of patients treated with the combo reached endoscopic remission—defined as the absence of visible inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract as observed during endoscopy or colonoscopy—compared to 21.3% of those on Skyrizi and 18% of patients on trosunilimab.
The gulf between remission rates seen in patients on ABBV-466 versus monotherapy groups further increased at week 24, AbbVie said, with 40.5% in the ABBV-466 group reaching this goal, as compared to 22.4% of patients treated only with Skyrizi and 20% of those on trosunilimab monotherapy.
As for safety, rates of serious adverse events (SAEs) were slightly higher for ABBV-466 at 10.4%, while 9.6% of patients on Skyrizi monotherapy and 9% of those given trosunilimab alone had SAEs. In the ABBV-466 and trosunilimab arms, the most common adverse events (AEs) were symptoms of Crohn’s disease and nausea. In the Skyrizi cohort, the most common AEs were Crohn’s symptoms and joint pain without inflammation, according to AbbVie.
The results were presented Monday as a late-breaker at the 2026 Annual United European Gastroenterology Week Congress (UEGW) in Barcelona.
In AbbVie’s press release, Kori Wallace, the company’s global head of immunology clinical development, touted the combo as an example of how the company is “building the next generation of our inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) portfolio, leveraging insights from our own research to address disease pathways that may remain active even when a central inflammatory pathway is inhibited.”
AbbVie’s research indicated evidence of α4β7-driven inflammation despite the IL-23 p19 inhibition driven by Skyrizi, leading the company to “augment” the drug with a novel α4β7 inhibitor, trosunilimab, Wallace continued.
“The TARGET-CD results reinforce our strategy of advancing therapies designed around the complex biology of Crohn’s disease,” she said.
BMO was bullish on the strategy. “Results are a positive for ABBV shares, potentially positioning the company with an efficacious follow-up molecule to Skyrizi in Crohn’s,” the analysts wrote.
AbbVie has previously been lauded for its lifecycle management. When Humira—once pharma’s top-selling drug—went off patent, AbbVie leaned on its new immunology stars, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, which in 2025 reeled in $17.5 billion and $8.3 billion, respectively.

Novartis will continue to study Fabhalta in other indications, with late-stage studies in two rare diseases—atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and generalized myasthenia gravis—expected to read out later this year and next year, respectively.
Novartis has pulled the plug on a Phase 2 study testing the complement blocker Fabhalta for patients with lupus that has inflamed the kidneys, a condition called lupus nephritis.
“The decision was based on strategic considerations and was not driven by any interim efficacy or safety findings,” a company spokesperson told BioSpace in an email. The study enrolled 81 patients with lupus nephritis, according to a federal clinical trials database .
The mid-stage study was originally designed to have two parts, this first of which compared Fabhalta, also known as iptacopan, plus standard of care against placebo plus standard of care. The second part was expected to have three arms testing iptacopan plus standard of care, iptacopan plus placebo and placebo plus standard of care. The primary outcome for both parts was percentage of patients achieving a complete renal response at week 24.
Novartis has completed the first portion of the study but has decided not to continue on with part two, the spokesperson said.
Fabhalta was first approved in late 2023 for a rare blood disorder called paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. The drug is a complement factor B inhibitor that tunes down activity of an immune pathway thought to contribute to disease activity when overactivated. In the following years, Fabhalta has also secured approvals in IgA nephropathy and complement 3 glomerulopathy .
Last year, Novartis reported $505 million in global sales for Fabhalta, up nearly 290% year-on-year, with growth driven by the drug’s continued strong uptake across indications.
Despite the termination of the mid-stage lupus nephritis study, “[i]ptacopan studies in other indications will continue as planned,” the spokesperson told BioSpace . Novartis has two Phase 3 studies for the drug in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, with one readout planned for this year and another for 2028, according to the pharma’s Q2 report . Fabhalta is also being studied for generalized myasthenia gravis, for which a late-stage data drop is expected next year.
In addition, Novartis is testing Fabhalta in several other ongoing programs, including for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis, intermediate age-related macular degeneration, pediatric C3 glomerulopathy, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and IgA nephropathy.
The fresh discontinuation also doesn’t mean that Novartis is giving up on lupus nephritis (LN). “Novartis remains committed to advancing LN research,” the spokesperson told BioSpace , pointing to the company’s ongoing Phase 3 study for the investigational monoclonal antibody ianalumab, for which data are expected in 2027, according to the Q2 report.
Fabhalta’s mid-stage study shuttering comes after Novartis in September stopped a mid-stage study for its TREM2 stabilizer lifonebart for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis—the pharma’s fourth trial stumble in just a month’s time. The pharma experienced high-profile clinical setbacks for the antibody-oligonucleotide conjugate del-desiran , the antisense therapy pelacarsen and the CAR T cell therapy rapcabtagene autoleucel .

Roche is offering $400 million upfront and over $15 billion in biobucks to team up with Hansoh Pharmaceutical in hopes of developing a portfolio of new antibody-drug conjugates using the latter’s in-house tech.
Roche is returning to China biotech partner Hansoh Pharmaceutical, expanding upon an antibody-drug conjugate alliance with a new, wide-ranging deal that could top $15 billion.
Roche has inked a licensing pact for a “broad portfolio” of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with several Hansoh subsidiaries, according to a stock exchange filing from Hansoh. The new deal encompasses two existing preclinical ADC programs, plus multiple programs based on Roche-proposed targets powered by Hansoh’s ADC platform technology.
Hansoh will be responsible for program development up to the completion of global Phase 1a trials, with Roche taking on further development outside of certain Asian territories, such as mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan.
Roche is doling out $400 million upfront, plus a $110 million payment at the one-year mark. The rest of the massive potential total could come by way of milestone payments. Hansoh will also have the chance to collect tiered royalties.
Hansoh could also choose to contribute to ex-Asia development for two programs stemming from the alliance and gain incremental earnings from potential U.S. commercialization.
The two companies previously paired up almost exactly a year ago, with Roche paying $80 million upfront for certain licensing rights to HS-20110, a CDH17-targeting ADC using a topoisomerase inhibitor payload to treat solid tumors.

Carrier Logistics is partnering with LSP44 to automate shipment tracking for less-than-truckload carriers, including requests that arrive without a tracking number or with an incorrect one. The companies are developing an AI -powered connection designed to reduce the emails and phone calls carrier customer service teams must handle.
What’s Related
The collaboration lets shippers and third-party logistics providers find shipments by matching information they already have with records in a carrier’s transportation management system . That system is the software carriers use to manage freight and shipment records.
The companies are addressing what Carrier Logistics President Ben Wiesen calls “AI bot fatigue.” When automated tracking requests fail, bots turn to carrier customer service teams for answers, adding more messages and calls for employees to sort through.
“3PLs and shippers use APIs for shipment tracking, and these APIs are successful a majority of the time but are open to failing due to missing or incorrect tracking numbers,” Wiesen said. “This is where the bots step in, resulting in intrusive emails and phone calls that overwhelm the customer service teams at motor carriers.”
Finding shipments without a tracking number
The new connection uses an application programming interface, or API, which lets software systems exchange information directly. Instead of requiring a correct tracking number for every request, the AI matches known shipment details with shipments recorded in the carrier’s system.
According to the companies, that matching process can automatically resolve uncertainty about which shipment a customer is asking about. Shippers and 3PLs can then retrieve tracking information through the API, reducing the need to contact a carrier’s staff.
“With CLI’s new, AI-powered API, LTL carriers can provide the visibility their customers need without the added administrative burden and cost,” Wiesen said.
Reducing work for carrier service teams
Carrier Logistics provides freight management software for LTL carriers and other transportation businesses . Chicago-based LSP44 provides AI agents and software connections for 3PLs, freight forwarders, and brokers.
The companies say their joint engineering work is intended to make automated tracking more reliable and improve the accuracy of information passed along to customers. For carrier service teams, the goal is to reduce requests that require employees to find a shipment manually.
“The industry has treated manual tracking requests as the cost of doing business for decades,” said Nick Ruggiero, head of product at LSP44. “Every carrier running LTL has a customer service team absorbing that cost today.”

The priciest Sorento for the US market is even pricier for 2027. Last year's EX with all-wheel drive used to retail at $48,290 from the outset, meaning that the 2027 model is a staggering $5,600 more expensive. You do get plenty of equipment for the money, beginning with the head-up display mentioned earlier. Customers who want the plug further get a heated steering wheel, heated second-row seats, and a panoramic sunroof.
Goodies also include ventilated and heated front seats, perforated leather across all three rows, 14-way power adjustments and a thigh extension for the driver's seat, 10-way power adjustments for the front passenger, second-row captain's chairs, and a split-folding third row for a grand total of six seats. X-Line embossing on the front seatbacks also needs mentioning, along with open-pore inlays.
The people sitting behind the first row are presented with retractable sunshades, while audio entertainment comes courtesy of a 12-speaker Bose system. Wireless phone charging and a power liftgate come along for the ride. Good for 31 miles (50 kilometers) of electric-only driving, the plug-in hybrid Sorento for the US market is equipped with a battery that nets just around 14 kilowatt-hours.
A Level 1/Level 2 charging cable is included, which is great to hear when the entire point of the Sorento PHEV involves plugging in. Instead of an eCVT, a six-speed tranny does the talking. Under the hood, you will find a familiar 1.6-liter turbocharged inline-four that wouldn't mean too much without electric assistance.

With a full tank of gas and a full charge of the high-voltage battery, the Sorento PHEV should be good for a combined range of 440 miles (708 kilometers). The X-Line treatment dresses the nicely equipped SX-Prestige with 19-inch wheels, darker exterior detailing, specific bumpers, and so forth. Also worth noting, Steel Gray is out in favor of Pale Gray in the paint color palette.
Offering nearly 7.0 inches (176 millimeters) of ground clearance, the Sorento PHEV is pretty smart as well, offering Highway Driving Assist 2 and rear parking collision avoidance. Techy highlights also include surround view and blind-spot monitoring. Of course, adaptive cruise control is a standard item as well.
The compact-ish third row of seats brings a compromise to the table, with Kia America listing 29.6 inches (752 millimeters) of legroom and 12.6 cubic feet (357 liters) of cargo space behind it. Cargo theft is costing businesses far more than the value of the stolen freight; loss of a single €5,000 parcel can potentially generate €35,000 in additional costs, as organised gangs and cybercriminals exploit vulnerabilities in Europe’s supply chains.
LivingPackets’ Hidden Cost of High-Value Delivery report, published today, estimates that every euro of direct loss carries four to seven euros in additional costs, including replacement, reshipping, dispute handling, and customer dissatisfaction.
Across 10,000 shipments of goods worth €5,000 each, a 0.1% incident rate would mean 10 losses, representing €50,000 in stolen goods, and up to €350,000 in hidden costs, the analysis, drawing on Logistics Bureau research, found.
Meanwhile, TAPA EMEA recorded more than €1bn in freight theft losses across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa in the 18 months to 30 June. Only 7.8% of the 58,661 reported incidents included a recorded loss value, suggesting the documented total significantly understates the problem.
“The problem is not marginal,” said LivingPackets.
In an interview with SNAP, TAPA’s UK lead for EMEA Harry Hughes said: “We’ve seen organised crime groups travelling two to three hundred miles to target specific vehicles. They know the routes. They know the transport companies that are moving them, the lanes they go on.”
Cargo theft methods include curtain slashing, entire loaded trailers taken from depots, and cyber-enabled fraud involving phishing emails, falsified collection documents, and manipulated delivery instructions.
Mr Hughes also warned: “Criminals are sometimes buying legimate carriers, trading as a legitimate carrier for two to three weeks and then disappearing with loads.”
LivingPackets argued that while conventional tracking could record where a parcel was scanned, it cannot necessarily establish what happened between scans, or identify where custody was compromised.
However, its technology embeds sensing, authentication, and event recording into reusable shipping boxes.
LivingPackets founder and executive chairman Alexander Cotte said: “If the shipment itself can tell us what happened, brands, carriers and insurers start from the same facts.”
The company said French telecoms operator SFR had seen loss and damage claims fall by 93% on the flows concerned, while a luxury jeweller recorded no losses on LivingPackets-managed shipments. Automotive parts shipper Cotrolia reportedly reduced its breakage rate from 30% to 1%.
The report advised the need for stronger carrier verification, secure parking, tighter control of collection instructions, and better shipment visibility as criminals exploit both physical and digital weaknesses across freight networks.
SNAP’s head of commercial for the UK and Ireland, Nick Long, urged that secure truck parking should be integral to fleet security and journey planning, rather than treated as an optional extra.

Land Rover Introduces Defender Alasia Pack in Europe, But Its Defender 90 Model Loses an Iconic Item

Photo: Land Rover
For one reason or the other, Land Rover has decided to announce the new Alasia Pack for the Old Continent's markets in Spain first, and we almost missed it as it flew under the radar in Spanish.
No worries, we’re ready to rectify that potential omission and let you know that JLR is offering something new on the Land Rover Defender in Europe while at the same time taking something away from the smallest member of the family, the Defender 90. By the way, JLR now has dedicated media portals to more than two brands.
That’s because they recently segmented Land Rover into Range Rover, Defender , and Discovery, while Jaguar remains a singular brand. There are also portals for JLR Classic, which is where all the retro-modern action takes place. Then they hid the new Land Rover Defender Alasia Pack in the Spanish-speaking area…
And that’s how we ended up almost missing the news. Anyway, as far as we can tell, since we’re not native Spanish speakers, the new Alasia Pack isn’t exclusive to Spain, and it will be offered throughout Europe, which is a good thing. The new style pack adds Cyprus Copper accents to the exterior, aiming to provide the British off-roader with a touch of elegance without actually taking way any of its off-road chops.
The styling setup is offered on all versions, like the Defender 90, 100, and 130, and has a Mediterranean-inspired finish focused on Cyprus - Alasia was the island's ancient name, and the metal has historical importance to the island of Cyprus, once shaping entire early civilizations. Now, the copper finish appears on the outside on the front grille bar, on the side vents, and the rear towing eyes. It's a subtle makeover, indeed.
The Alasia Pack is now available to order across Europe for the Defender 90, 110, and 130, but Land Rover hasn’t announced any pricing details. This option does join the brand's growing range of customization choices, and if that’s not enough, it turns out that the small Defender 90 can now loose on of its defining exterior traits: the giant spare wheel sitting on its rear door.
Yep, as it turns out, instead of giving you something, Land Rover is taking away a feature – it’s all in the name of safety, as it allegedly improves rear visibility for the smallest member of the family. So, there’s now a spare wheel removal kit up for order in Europe, which takes away one of the SUV’s defining features for additional visibility and easier maneuvering in tight spaces.
Land Rover didn’t even bother to design a separate fifth door without spare-wheel mounting points, but that would've added cost issues – now you’ll be stuck with your friends worrying that someone stole the spare wheel off your precious Defender 90, probably…

Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 19, 2026
Ivanhoe Electric (NYSE-A, TSX: IE) is in advanced negotiations to sell copper from its $1.4-billion Santa Cruz project in Arizona as surging demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure and power grids intensifies competition for United States supplies.
The company has attracted interest from traditional commodity traders and strategic partners seeking domestic copper supplies, CEO Taylor Melvin told Bloomberg News . He declined to identify the prospective buyers but said offtake agreements could include financing to help develop the mine.
“We need a lot more than Santa Cruz to fill that gap,” Melvin told the newswire, referring to the widening divide between U.S. copper demand and domestic production.
The negotiations come as copper prices hover near record highs and major technology companies seek to secure supplies for data centres and electricity networks. Global demand growth is expected to outpace production, increasing pressure on the U.S. to develop new mines and reduce its reliance on imported metal.
Financing talks
U.S. President Donald Trump publicly backed financing for Santa Cruz during an Aug. 7 mining roundtable at the State Department, highlighting the project’s importance to efforts to expand domestic mineral production.
That same month, Ivanhoe Electric received a Preliminary Project Letter (PPL) from the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM Bank) outlining up to $1.1 billion in potential debt financing . The letter represents a preliminary step rather than a final loan commitment.
The company is also discussing project financing with about a dozen commercial banks, Melvin said.
Santa Cruz could become one of the first major new U.S. copper mines in nearly two decades. A preliminary feasibility study released last year estimated initial development costs at $1.24 billion, while the more recent figure for the project’s first phase stands at $1.4 billion. First production is targeted for 2029.
Melvin said the project, combined with nearby resources, could eventually establish one of the country’s leading copper-producing regions.
The financing discussions highlight the capital requirements facing U.S. copper developers as they seek to bring new production online. Potential supply agreements could provide an additional source of funding, although Ivanhoe has yet to announce binding deals.
Technology advantage
Santa Cruz plans to use an on-site processing method that produces copper cathode, a refined form of the metal that can be manufactured into wire, cable and foil. Ivanhoe has promoted the approach as part of its strategy to develop a lower-emissions operation.
The technology could appeal to buyers seeking more direct access to finished copper products while reducing the need for conventional processing facilities.
Major technology companies are already exploring alternative production methods to secure future supplies. Earlier this year, Amazon agreed to purchase copper from Gunnison Copper ‘s (TSX: GCU; US-OTC: GCUMF) Arizona mine using proprietary leaching technology developed by Rio Tinto (ASX, LSE: RIO).
The process avoids conventional smelting and refining, with the resulting copper destined for Amazon’s data centres.
For Ivanhoe, securing customers and financing will be crucial to advancing Santa Cruz toward its planned 2029 start-up. The project’s development timeline also underscores the challenge facing the global copper industry: demand is accelerating faster than new domestic mines can be brought into production.

With equipment and options comparable to MANA (this boat specifically), that brings it to approximately $3.48 million before import-related costs. Once freight, duties, tariffs and applicable taxes are factored in, the estimated landed cost in Florida is approximately $4.13 million."
I'm not an expert in yacht depreciation, but I see no reason why this shouldn't have sold for at least $2 million, given the information provided by the dealer. But do let me know how much you guys think this is worth.
The thing is, boats are in a whole different league than cars, and I'm not just talking about base prices, but also running costs, not to mention docking and mooring fees. It depends on which marina you use. If you live in Miami, you can expect to pay somewhere on the higher end of the spectrum. It's not Monaco, but it's pretty much the same as in Southern California. Expensive.
To be fair, there's no telling where this boat will end up. The buyer doesn't necessarily need to be from southern Florida. There's a lot of coastline surrounding the continental United States, and it's common practice to buy a boat from dock X and then ship it across the country to wherever it is that you hang your pirate's hook.

Of course, the battery-less versions aren’t really intended for someone buying their first Monarc. Instead, the company is targeting existing owners who already have compatible batteries and chargers sitting around.
That makes sense, since when the company first launched its premier e-bikes earlier this year , it did so with an impressively high-value package that included not just one but two batteries. At the time, it was seen as a bold move – especially since many e-bike companies hold back spare batteries as a significant upsell opportunity. But in this case, it looks like Monarc was angling for a different strategy more akin to the power tool world: build all your products around a single battery and then let owners swap just a few batteries among them.
If you already own a Monarc and want to add a second bike for a spouse, family member, or just a different style of riding, why buy another battery and charger if you don’t need them?
It’s a surprisingly logical idea, even if “battery-less e-bike” sounds like an oxymoron at first.
The one-battery option will likely have even broader appeal. While Monarc has traditionally included two batteries with its e-bikes, which was great for riders who want maximum range, not everyone wanted or needed a spare battery. And since batteries are also the single most expensive component on an e-bike, offering the models with a single battery is a great way to reduce cost and save owners money.
For riders who generally take shorter trips and can simply recharge at home, dropping the second battery saves $250 without changing anything about the bike itself.
Monarc launched earlier this year, coming out swinging hard with higher quality e-bikes than we’ve typically seen from direct-to-consumer companies, yet at prices that put bike shop brands to shame.
I’ve personally had the chance to get a much closer look at Monarc than I’ve often gotten with most e-bike companies. Earlier this year, I visited the company’s headquarters in Minnesota, where I met the team, saw its operation firsthand, and even chatted with members of its in-house customer service team between their customer service calls.
I’ll have an in-depth video and article on that experience soon, but suffice it to say that my detailed visit helped drive home what Monarc is trying to do differently.
The company is essentially attempting to offer the type of nicer, more premium e-bike experience we normally associate with much more expensive brands, but using a direct-to-consumer model to keep the prices considerably lower.
That’s an increasingly difficult needle to thread in the e-bike industry. There are plenty of cheap direct-to-consumer e-bikes available online, just as there are plenty of polished premium e-bikes sold through dealers for several thousand dollars. Trying to land somewhere between those two worlds – better bikes and real support without premium-bike pricing – is a much smaller target. But with the backing of its parent company Lectric Ebikes, which happens to be the largest e-bike company in North America, Monarc seems to have stuck the landing gracefully.
The brand has impressed me so far with how seriously the team seems to take its mission. It’s one thing to put a customer service email address on a website. It’s another to walk into a company’s headquarters and see the people actually answering those emails and phone calls, sometimes jogging over to the engineering team to ensure they’ve got the most up-to-date tech answers for customers.
The new battery pricing strategy is another interesting example of the company thinking a bit differently.
Monarc calls its traditional two-battery package “The Monarc Way,” and that remains the full-monty option for riders who want the most range and flexibility.
The new single-battery version, dubbed “Monarc Base,” is designed for riders who simply don’t need as much battery capacity and would rather keep another $250 in their pockets.
Then there’s “The Second Monarc,” which includes neither a battery nor charger. That one is specifically aimed at current Monarc owners who can share batteries between bikes.
And personally, I really like the concept. I have just two Ryobi batteries but probably six or seven Ryobi power tools. I’m not really doing a lot of sanding and angle grinding at the same time, so it makes sense. And in the same way you’re probably not commuting and mountain-biking at the same time, this model gives Monarc a way to let riders tackle different e-biking scenarios without the extra cost of several redundant batteries sitting on the shelf.
We’ve seen e-bike companies increasingly lock riders into proprietary battery ecosystems, but there can actually be an upside to that ecosystem once you own multiple compatible bikes. If you’ve already got two perfectly good batteries sitting in your garage, forcing you to buy two more just because you want another bike doesn’t make much sense.
The $500 savings also makes Monarc’s pricing quite a bit more interesting. A $1,399 Tracer or $1,499 Marker sounds considerably different from an e-bike pushing two grand, even if you obviously need to already have a battery to make those prices useful. And to be perfectly honest, those bikes have no business costing that little, especially when you consider the higher end parts like Shimano CUES transmissions, Talon P4 quad-piston brakes, GNEISS reverse arch suspension forks, Bafang 750W motors, and other high-end parts adorning the bikes. These are budget bikes prices for more premium-end gear.
For first-time buyers, I suspect the $250 savings on the single-battery models will be the more meaningful development. Many riders simply don’t need two batteries, and now they don’t have to pay for capacity they aren’t going to use.
So yes, Monarc is now selling e-bikes without batteries.
But rather than another case of an e-bike company finding something to remove from the box to advertise a lower price, this one actually seems to make sense.

Subaru is testing its own tech for its next-generation EVs, breaking away from its longstanding partnership with Toyota.
Subaru moves away from Toyota for its next EV
After falling behind Chinese brands like BYD and other emerging EV makers like Tesla, Subaru and Toyota revealed plans in 2024 to co-develop four new electric SUVs by each brand by the end of 2026, including the updated Solterra and bZ4X ( now the bZ in the US).
The partnership was designed to share development costs and manufacturing space to cut costs and speed up development.
Subaru is now preparing to branch off from its partnership with Toyota for its next-generation electric vehicles as it looks to establish its own brand in the EV space.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
According to Automotive News , Subaru revealed its latest in-house tech on Sunday that will power its upcoming next-generation electric vehicles.
“By developing vehicles in-house and having EV technologies on our own, we can quickly deliver to our customers the peace of mind and driving pleasure that define Subaru,” said Takatomo Watamori, executive officer in charge of engineering.
2027 Subaru Trailseeker (Source: Subaru)
The new tech includes Subaru’s first dedicated EV platform, plus new batteries, electric motors, and an integrated control unit to enable over-the-air updates.
Subaru showed a prototype to reporters at its test course just north of Tokyo. The camouflaged test mule used an all-wheel-drive powertrain with a combined 509 horsepower (380 kW). Subaru said the new setup enables the EV to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under 4 seconds.
While it didn’t reveal a specific launch date, company executives said some of the new tech will begin rolling out around 2029.
2027 Subaru Solterra EV (Source: Subaru)
The prototype featured the new platform mounted under the body of an Outback. It used an e-axle developed with Toyota’s supplier Aisin Group and a battery pack from Panasonic Energy.
Subaru said the components are lighter, smaller, and more efficient than those used in its current electric vehicles.
Subaru’s engineers say the motors deliver a 30% efficiency increase compared with the industry average. The battery pack, meanwhile, uses 4,000 cylindrical cells from Panasonic Energy. It’s 24% lighter than the previous pack, and Subaru aims for an energy density 20% higher than the industry average.
Subaru Trailseeker EV interior (Source: Subaru)
Although it used an Outback as a test mule, Subaru quickly clarified that the design is not final and could change for the production version.
Subaru is developing an in-house integrated ECU that will support over-the-air (OTA) updates and integrate its EyeSight advanced driver assistance system.
By streamlining them across its lineup, Subaru said the new ECUs will help reduce costs. It will also develop a custom chip with Advanced Micro Devices that will utilize artificial intelligence in future EyeSight updates.
Subaru has big ambitions. By the first half of the 2030s, it aims to deliver 1.2 million vehicles, topping its record of 1.1 million in 2018. Last year, it sold about 924,000 vehicles, a fraction of Toyota’s at over 11 million.

source_document.body:
A view of the mill at the Galena complex in Idaho. Credit: Americas Gold and Silver.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 19, 2026
Americas Gold and Silver (TSX: USA; NYSE-A: USAS) reported weaker-than-expected silver production in the third quarter amid ongoing infrastructure work at its main Galena complex in Idaho.
Silver production in the three months ended Sept. 30 hit a record 800,458 oz., a 4.6% increase from the same quarter a year ago, Americas Gold said Monday in a statement . Financial analysts who follow the company had forecast median production of 950,000 ounces.
Americas Gold nevertheless reaffirmed its earlier goal of producing 3.2 million to 3.6 million oz. of silver for all of 2026 at all-in sustaining costs of $30 to $35 per ounce. Silver production through nine months stands at 2.3 million oz., “which continues to be in line with our 2026 expectations,” CEO Paul André Huet said.
Full-year production will be weighted to the second half of the year with associated lower costs, Huet added.
“We have a negative read on the results; while the guidance reiteration is encouraging, Galena underperformed our expectations and USA will need to produce about 1.1 million oz. in the fourth quarter, up 43% quarter-on-quarter, to achieve the midpoint of guidance,” Desjardins Capital Markets mining analyst Bryce Adams said Monday in a note.
Americas Gold stock fell 0.4% to C$5.32 Monday morning in Toronto, having earlier touched C$5.25. The company has a market capitalization of about C$1.8 billion ($1.3 million).
Record sales
Silver sales hit a record 860,850 oz. in the period, exceeding production by about 7.5%, Americas Gold said.
Copper production reached 918,456 lb., while antimony sales totalled 121,691 pounds. The company also produced 964,551 lb. of lead.
Americas Gold is advancing several infrastructure projects at Galena. They include construction of a paste fill plant, upgrades to a hoist and installation of underground fibre optic communications.
Underground waste development is also progressing to prepare higher-grade silver-copper-antimony veins for future long-hole stoping.
Galena produced 384,579 oz. of silver during the period, while sales totalled 437,709 ounces. The operation is recovering from temporary production interruptions in the second quarter.
The mine also produced 964,551 lb. of lead, 182,362 lb. of copper and 101,011 lb. of antimony.
Mexico increase
Americas Gold’s Cosalá operation in Mexico’s Sinaloa state produced 415,879 oz. of silver during the quarter, a 23% jump from the previous three months. Silver sales hit 423,141 ounces.
The increase in output at Cosalá reflected stronger grades as mining advanced into the heart of the EC120 orebody, supported by improved underground material movement.
Cosalá also produced 736,094 lb. of copper during the quarter, accounting for most of the company’s consolidated copper production.
Americas Gold ended September with an unaudited cash balance of $63 million and available liquidity of $113 million. That included $50 million under an existing credit facility.

Ares Management has agreed to buy Infinity Transportation, a railcar and intermodal equipment leasing company, from KKR for about $2.9 billion, the companies announced Monday.
What’s Related
Infinity owns and manages about 50,000 railcars. It leases them to more than 350 customers in the U.S., Canada and Mexico .
The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending approvals and other standard conditions. Ares Infrastructure Equity and Ares Insurance Solutions will manage the funds for the purchase.
“Infinity’s railcar portfolio is a critical component of the U.S. transportation and logistics supply chain,” said Mike Roth, partner in Ares Infrastructure Equity, and Anup Agarwal, head and chief investment officer of Ares Insurance Solutions.
Why Ares did the deal
Ares plans to fund growth in Infinity’s fleet and pursue more acquisitions once the deal closes. Roth and Agarwal pointed to reshoring , new domestic industrial investment, and the push for sturdier supply chains as reasons they expect railcar demand to hold up over the long run. They also said the deal builds on Ares’ growing activity in the rail sector.
Infinity was founded in 2004 and is based in Atlanta. KKR, through its Global Atlantic subsidiary, has been invested in the company since 2016. Starting in 2021, KKR helped Infinity build out its own standalone operation, grow its fleet and raise its value by 150%.
“We appreciate KKR’s partnership and support, which enabled us to invest in the team, expand our fleet and build Infinity into the industry leader it is today,” said Jeff Edelman, president and CEO of Infinity. Edelman added that he’s looking forward to starting a new chapter with Ares.
Macquarie Capital and Simpson Thacher & Bartlett advised KKR on the sale. Citi and Kirkland & Ellis advised Ares.

The U.S. Army’s program for accelerating new technologies announced the winners of a humanoid robot competition , which assessed how the emerging technology could contribute to future military operations.
According to the Sept. 29 announcement , the five winners of the Army’s xTechHumanoid competition include ACES Group, IHMC Robotics, Hydroplane Limited, Ras Labs and Velocity Explorations.
Alex Miller, the Army’s chief technology officer, explained that through the program, the service tried to identify “the problems, mission needs, and opportunities” humanoid robots could best be used.
“xTech is our method of surveying the industry landscape and fast-tracking promising technology rather than falling victim to years-long studies,” Miller said.
“Humanoid robots are part of a broader autonomy push to increase the depth and breadth of robotic platforms and components industry can provide for a range of missions,” he added.
The expectation
For the competition, Army officials reviewed each company’s white paper proposal for its humanoid robot. They evaluated the concepts based on several criteria, including military utility, technical merit and technological maturity.
Of the 103 submissions, the Army selected 10 finalists, each of which received $25,000. The service then identified five winners through a live experimentation event.
According to the 2025 competition announcement , the event tested the robots on a series of collective tasks “in the context of a military small unit mission conducted in a combat situation.”
During the event, officials also reviewed the baseline system capabilities and advanced subsystems.
Examples of the former include checkpoint security, gap crossing or obstacle clearing and firefighting. Whereas the latter included technologies like thermal sensors, battery life and autonomy.
The reality
However, Robert Griffin, a senior researcher at IHMC Robotics , told Military Times that the competition’s individual requirements exceeded what current technology could achieve.
“The individual things that were outlined were, in any one element, beyond what is possible given the current state of the art,” Griffin said.
Companies compete in the U.S. Army's xTechHumanoid finals at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Connor Taggert/U.S. Army)
“For example, you don’t have a robot that can run 28 miles an hour while carrying 50 pounds and operating for 24 hours,” he said. “It’s not a thing that exists in the world.”
Because the Army’s “actual full desirements were beyond what can currently be done,” Griffin said, developers had to prioritize different elements of their robots’ capabilities for the demonstrations.
Griffin’s team focused on baseline capabilities.
“The big thing for us was to have the robot show up at the competition, move around in the world, unsupported, at a reasonable pace, and then respond to commands,” he said.
Video of the competition shows IHMC’s robot “Alex” following voice commands directing it to walk through a field and then, under the control of a human with a remote, through the woods and across gravel.
Alex also grasps a small shovel, begins to dig and attempts to pour dirt into a bucket. Although it doesn’t succeed, it demonstrates the movement. And finally, Alex collapses and has to be transported out on a gurney.
Testing subsystems
Other competitors focused on subsystems.
Hydroplane and ACES Group competed with their batteries, while Velocity Explorations entered software that enabled its robot to listen to radio traffic between people and understand their movements and tasks. Using that information to develop an understanding of the broader battlespace, the platform could then determine how to act.
Ras Labs tested highly sensitive fingertip tactile sensors that allowed a robot to handle delicate objects.
While multiple companies said they participated because it was a chance to test their products, Dr. Anita Sengupta, Hydroplane’s founder and chief executive, explained that her company has traditionally done work for large structures and aircraft, but recently started working on smaller and portable systems.
“We saw a good overlap between developing a power system for a humanoid, whether it’s a person or a robot, as well as the drone use case, so it just seemed like an interesting use case for us to take our technology to,” she said.
For the competition, her company adapted a 10-kilowatt system originally designed for the Marine Corps in 2024, but made it smaller because the humanoid only needed a few kilowatts. The device utilizes a fuel cell similar to what a generator uses, but instead of using diesel fuel, it uses hydrogen. Sengupta explained that the benefits are that it has about three times the energy density and a higher conversion efficiency.
Although Hydroplane didn’t directly power a humanoid robot with its fuel cell, the Army tested it to see if it could power a humanoid robot. In turn, Hydroplane helped establish those standards, with the intent to eventually collaborate with a humanoid robot team.
The future
In the recent announcement, the Army said the competition revealed a clear picture of “both the progress commercial industry has made in humanoid robotics and the technical challenges that remain.” The findings, the service said, will help it direct research toward technologies that offer the greatest return for warfighters.
Companies compete in the U.S. Army's xTechHumanoid finals at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Connor Taggert/U.S. Army)
But while humanoid robots might eventually take on more complex military tasks, Griffin said the industry is still a long way from developing machines like Arnold Schwarzenegger’s T-800 from The Terminator franchise.
“I don’t think that any person who has a modicum of ethics is going to say that we need to be having these robots making life or death decisions,” he said, noting how easily current AI models can be confused or manipulated.
Instead, Griffin said the future of humanoid robotics will depend in part on what investors want the machines to do. Industrial companies, for example, may see opportunities to automate tasks typically performed by humans.
“Our goal is to be able to make robots that remove people from having to do harmful tasks,” he said about his company, pointing to scenarios such as first responders entering burning buildings and nuclear cleanup.
About Daniel Terrill
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

Silence Therapeutics’ lead siRNA asset for the rare blood cancer polycythemia vera has been earning analyst raves in a tight race to challenge Takeda in a potential $2 billion market.
Germany’s Merck KGaA is making a commotion in the rare disease space with the $1.1 billion acquisition of RNA specialist Silence Therapeutics and the biotech’s Phase 3 asset for polycythemia vera divesiran.
The deal gives Merck KGaA “an entry point into hematology,” Danny Bar-Zohar, member of the pharma’s executive board and CEO of healthcare, said in a Monday statement.
U.K.-based Silence focuses on short interfering RNA (siRNA), developing therapies designed to quiet disease-associated genes without permanently altering DNA.
Silence investors will receive $20 per share, representing an 82% premium on the biotech’s 30-day average price of $10.99, according to a Monday press release . The $1.1 billion represents the enterprise value while Merck KGaA noted that the equity value is about $1.3 billion. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.
“We believe that the deal makes sense for Silence ADS holders given the interest in divesiran in polycythemia vera (PV) and need to conduct a Phase III trial in a competitive space with likely new CEO leadership,” William Blair wrote Monday morning.
Mergers & acquisitions
5 SMID-Cap Pharmas Poised for M&A Action
Mergers and acquisitions are not just for Big Pharma. A new report from Leerink Partners takes a stab at identifying the small- to mid-cap pharmas best prepared to bolster their pipelines with a buyout.
October 29, 2025
·
7 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
Silence has been helmed by interim executive officer Iain Ross since December 2025, when CEO Craig Tooman agreed to depart the company.
Merck KGaA will gain a clutch of rare disease assets, including divesiran, which is currently in Phase 2 development for PV and in earlier-stage research for other blood disorders. Silence also has four cardiometabolic programs, led by mid-stage candidate zerlasiran.
Silence also has a partnership with AstraZeneca to develop therapies for cardiovascular, cardiometabolic, renal and respiratory diseases. The pharma recently handed Silence back the rights to SLN312, which is in Phase 1 testing for dyslipidemia.
Merck KGaA’s recent deals have centered on the rare disease space, including the 2025 acquisition of SpringWorks Therapeutics that delivered a drug for the rare tumor disease neurofibromatosis.
“Following the acquisition of SpringWorks Therapeutics last year, we continue to transform our pipeline toward areas of high specialization and unmet medical need, with an ongoing commitment to external innovation,” Kai Beckmann, chairman of Merck KGaA’s executive board and group CEO, said on Monday. “The proposed transaction follows our strategic priority to address attractive end markets also through M&A, creating value over the mid- to long-term.”
Indeed, analysts pointed to Merck KGaA as a likely buyer a year ago after the pharma suffered a series of clinical blows, such as the failure and discontinuation of evobrutinib in multiple sclerosis.
The deal comes just as Silence’s rival in PV, Disc Medicine, scored a major clinical win in erythropoietic protoporphyria. The two have been trading clinical data in PV, with analysts declaring Silence’s divesiran the likely front runner in the race to market. PV is a rare type of blood cancer, or chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm, characterized by the proliferation of red blood cells that can lead to elevated hematocrit levels. This can in turn lead to an increased risk of death from cardiovascular and thrombotic events.
Cancer
Disc sets up polycythemia vera challenge but Silence maintains lead
The polycythemia vera field is heating up, with Disc Medicine and Silence Therapeutics each advancing next-generation therapies, playing catch-up to Takeda and Protagonist Therapeutics, who won the FDA’s approval last month for Mimrylo.
September 11, 2026
·
2 min read

In August, Silence reported that divesiran led to an 88% clinical response rate in treated patients, compared with 19% in placebo controls, during the Phase 2 SANRECO trial. William Blair declared the results “best-in-field” for PV.
Divesiran is designed to silence the TMPRSS6 gene, which is involved in the regulation of hepcidin that the body uses as a regulator of iron metabolism, Merck KGaA explained in the release. By increasing hepcidin levels, the drug limits iron availability for red blood cell production. This should reduce the need for frequent blood withdrawals that patients undergo as a form of treatment.
Also in SANRECO, divesiran resulted in 0.2 blood draws per patient as compared to 2.1 for those who received placebo through week 36.
Silence was also facing Takeda, which achieved approval for Mimrylo in PV this August. The Japanese company has forecast peak sales of $1-2 billion for the asset. William Blair said Merck KGaA appears to have gotten a bit of a deal given Silence also comes with a broader technology platform.
“The deal valuation does appear inexpensive considering Merck KGaA also gets the broader mRNAi GOLD siRNA platform as well,” the firm wrote. “However, this deal takes the execution risk off the table in an increasingly competitive space and delivers near-term shareholder value from what appears to be a competitive bid process.”

U.S. Army Soldiers assigned to 25th Combat Aviation Brigade, 25th Infantry Division, conduct an experimental over water gunnery exercise in a CH-47 Chinook over the Pacific Ocean, Sept. 29, 2026. U.S. Army's expanded rapid-fielding and modernization initiative is designed to test and integrate emerging technologies directly with soldiers in active formations. (U.S. Army photo by Capt. Katie Kolb)
Disruption by adversaries and the inherent unreliability of network infrastructure in the Pacific make building a reliable network infrastructure a major challenge for the US Army.
Overcoming that challenge can be the difference between being able to operate across all domains or face potential blind spots, affecting logistics, movement and combat operations, said Doug Jones, chief technology officer for defense at Leidos .
“I look at it through three lenses,” he said. “First, it’s a high-end fight with a mixture of exquisite weapons and mass. It’s not one or the other, which we’ve seen in some other domain scenarios. Second, it’s contested across all domains – space, cyber, air, sea, land. Those are areas that we are often historically dominant. It’s against an adversary force that’s been expressly created to counter how we project power.
“We project power typically through our carrier forces, through our air forces, through how we defend and launch land forces, and through cyber and information dominance. We have to be able to counter all those. From an Army perspective, we have to be able to secure all those critical nodes in the Pacific so that we can project that power across those domains.”
Maintaining the ability to deter adversaries and project power requires reliable infrastructure, strong partnerships with regional allies, and robust logistics capabilities. Although water dominates the Pacific, land operations remain critical.
US Army paratroopers assigned to the 11th Airborne Division board a US Air Force C-130J Super Hercules, assigned to the 36th Airlift Squadron, for airdrop training in support of Orient Shield 2026, at Yokota Air Base, Japan, Sept. 15, 2026. (US Air Force photo by Senior Airman Cayla Hunt.)
Building the foundation
The Army needs a dependable network no matter where it is operating, but the characteristics of the Pacific make that a more complicated challenge than in other areas. Network infrastructure in the region is often inherently unreliable, especially in the island chains, and can easily be disrupted by weather. Those characteristics force a new way of thinking about building a reliable infrastructure, said Eric Moore, senior vice president and business area lead for Leidos digital military services solutions.
“In other theaters we can oftentimes design systems around some degree of relatively stable fiber, data center, commercial connectivity for multi-path solutions, but it’s based on some degree of fixed asset that exists in the theater that we can then leverage when bringing capabilities to the fight,” said Moore. “In this theater we have to think more about deployable and reconstitutable assets.”
Moore said that the focus needs to be on leveraging the land masses that do exist in the Pacific to be able to deploy services there when they are needed. By building a more diverse set of resources that can be mobile, the Army can take the network with it while operating in the Pacific, allowing for connectivity even in areas where there is not an existing infrastructure that can be counted on.
While there are solutions that can enable portable network capabilities, the Army also has to be prepared for the possibility that forces will be operating without connectivity or with limited connectivity for extended periods of time. Because there are fewer network paths available in the region compared to other theaters such as Europe, the Army will need to be able to work around connectivity challenges while maintaining information dominance.
“Connectivity cannot be a prerequisite for mission success. The Army must be prepared to operate, communicate and make critical decisions in environments where networks are degraded, disrupted or completely unavailable for extended periods,” said Moore. Maintaining information dominance means building resilience into every layer of the mission – ensuring Soldiers have access to the data, intelligence and capabilities they need to act decisively, even when disconnected.”
Not just water
The first thing that comes to mind about the Pacific is the vast expanses of water in the region. But as previously mentioned, land masses are key in the region, as well, as establishing footholds on islands makes it possible to support forces as they move throughout the region.
“You have to control and protect all the land assets in the theater,” said Jones. “That’s critical to the Army because they’re running the logistics. They’re doing integrated air missile defense and base defense. And then they may be doing long-range attacks, whether it’s Army assets or enabling air assets or supporting maritime assets and defending them as they’re transiting. This is not a new challenge from a logistics standpoint. During World War II, the US had to create bases as it hopped from island to island to enable the logistics needed for combat operations. But with forces now dependent on real-time information gathering and data analysis, it’s not just moving troops and materiel. It’s enabling connectivity wherever forces are, and ensuring that connectivity can stand up to jamming or disruption.
“We can’t just rely on single monolithic systems,” said Moore. “It’s not resiliency that can be bought through a single system. It comes from diversity of solution, diversity of transport, diversity of storage, diversity of underlying capabilities that enable the resiliency that supports defense against the threat.”
The Army is focusing on building a transport-agnostic underlying network, with the goal of implementing a network foundation in the Pacific comparable to the United States or Europe that can support logistics, communications and command-and-control needs in the Pacific theater. Leidos supports this effort through its work on the Army’s Global Unified Network (AGUN) modernization contract, which uses software-defined network technology to help build a standardized infrastructure for global communication efforts.
“That ultimately is the fabric that is designed to provide the secure, resilient, data-centric transport layer that is multipath, inherently resilient and allows us to extend the Army’s enterprise capability out into this reconstitutable and deployable edge that is ultimately going to be required in the Pacific theater,” said Moore.
The importance of partnerships
While the Army works with allies across the world in organizations like NATO partnerships in the Pacific are a different situation because there is no Pacific equivalent of NATO. Partnerships between allied countries are driven more by personal relationships and collaboration as opposed to a formal structure for an alliance.
Working together to collect and share information is a cornerstone of those partnerships, and doing so requires an information architecture that allows for sharing of data. It also requires managing data at different levels of classification data, enabling sharing information without giving away sources and methods or running the risk of classified data being shared over unclassified networks.
Jones offered the example of signal processing and identifying air tracks to determine if they are potential threats such as adversary planes or weapons such as missiles. While the US has extensive capabilities to identify and track potential targets, many of its techniques to do so are classified. But data can be aggregated from a number of sources and shared in a way that provides information to allies without giving away sensitive information about how the data was gathered and interpreted, Jones said.
“You have commercial radars operating on some of these islands. We may be fusing military grade radars with them, both class and unclass. How do you pull those different pictures together and share that back with the partner nations, so that they can defend aspects of their solution?”
Cooperation in the Pacific has been long-running in some cases – e.g., the US’s long relationship with South Korea – and newer with other countries. Building and maintaining relationships in the region enables not only better information sharing, but also helps from a logistical standpoint, allowing access to island chains and protecting supply lines.
“It is a critical piece of how we’re going to be successful in the theater and we talked about how important all those island land masses are to be successful. We have to create those relationships with all these different areas,” Jones said. “That’s something that the nation’s been doing at a political level, but also at an infrastructure level as we work across the region.”
Defense needs
While the communications infrastructure in the Pacific is important for logistics and offensive operations, it is also critical to defense in the region. Whether it’s air-and-missile-defense, defending against maritime threats or protecting supply lines, reliable communications are needed.
Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have revealed some important lessons, but they don’t always apply to the Pacific given its characteristics.
“It’s a land battle,” said Jones. “These Class 1 UAS’s that are carrying a grenade aren’t going to operate well when you’re talking about islands that are minimum 50 to 75 miles apart, oftentimes hundreds to thousands of miles apart.”
One of the important lessons that does apply, however, is mobility. As has been repeatedly shown in both Ukraine and the Middle East, stationary targets such as TPY-2 radars can be damaged or destroyed by drone swarms and mass-missile attacks that overwhelm defenses.
Mobility means portable network capabilities, as well, which reinforces the need for a data infrastructure that can support forces on the move.

Disc Medicine’s bitopertin—rejected by the FDA in February—significantly reduced levels of a key disease biomarker and significantly increased the time patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria were able to spend in the sun and artificial light.
Disc Medicine’s bitopertin helped patients with a rare disorder that causes painful sensitivity to the sun spend more time in the light during a pivotal trial, setting the drug up for another attempt at an FDA approval after an accelerated application was rejected last year .
When the results were unblinded “a few days ago,” Disc CEO John Quisel was “overjoyed, as was our whole team,” he told BioSpace in an interview. “Just thrilled to be able to deliver a set of clean results in a set of endpoints that can be tricky.” The results, announced on Monday, revealed that the Phase 3 APOLLO trial hit all primary and secondary endpoints.
Prior to the results, analysts from BMO Capital Markets were optimistic that the readout could clear the way for a regulatory approval in erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP). Senior Biopharma Analyst Evan Seigerman told BioSpace that the firm believed there was a high probability that APOLLO would deliver.
Seigerman said bitopertin’s established ability to lower PPIX and the APOLLO trial’s sunlight-exposure endpoint could give Disc a clear path back to regulators. Pivotal rare disease trials are designed to show clear clinical benefit, Seigerman explained. “If that trial hits, then there’s a real path forward for approval.”
The regulatory road for bitopertin to this point has been tricky. In its complete response letter (CRL), revealed in a February 13 SEC filing by Disc, the FDA questioned the biotech’s use of a surrogate endpoint—percent change in whole-blood metal-free protoporphyrin IX (PPIX), the toxic metabolite that drives the disease—as a reasonable predictor of clinical benefit in EPP.
“The percent change in PPIX was relatively modest,” the agency wrote in the CRL, noting that it is unknown whether such magnitude of biomarker effect “is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit.”
Bitopertin was one of the first recipients of the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher in October 2025, granted to products that align with certain national priorities, such as meeting a large unmet medical need or boosting domestic manufacturing. A CNPV entitles the product to a drastically shortened review period of one to two months, down from the typical 10–12 months—but it does not guarantee approval.
In June, Disc announced it had reached an agreement with the FDA whereby the regulator would allow the use of the ongoing APOLLO trial, if successful, to support another regulatory filing for bitopertin. With the new data in hand, Disc plans to resubmit its application—this time for traditional approval of bitopertin—to the FDA by end of the year.

Bitopertin soars in Phase 3
The APOLLO trial, which enrolled 183 adults and adolescents with EPP, showed that bitopertin reduced PPIX by 41.4% compared to placebo (p-value < 0.0001) and increased time patients were able to spend in the light by 12.2 hours during month six (p-value = 0.0010), meeting the study’s two co-primary endpoints with what Quisel called a “high” degree of statistical significance.
All secondary endpoints were also positive, Disc said, including a statistically significant reduction in phototoxic reactions—which Quisel described as “horrifically painful” attacks where the skin is damaged—and increased light tolerance. Exploratory measures of quality-of-life improvement were also statistically significant.
As to the pain attacks, Quisel elaborated on the experience patients have relayed to Disc. “What patients tell us is it feels like they’re being burned or cooked from the inside, because this chemical, PPIX, is floating around in their blood, and when it’s activated by the light, it literally is burning them from the inside.” Many patients receive opioids, even though they don’t address the pain effectively, he added.
Bitopertin was generally well-tolerated with no new safety signals observed in APOLLO, according to Disc’s press release. Dizziness was the most common treatment-emergent adverse event, with 50% of patients in the treatment group experiencing this side effect, but the cases were mild to moderate and generally transient, the company said.
In addition, there were no study discontinuations in the bitopertin arm of the study, “which is remarkable for a six-month study,” Quisel said.
Collectively, the results will support a fresh new drug application for bitopertin. When that filing reaches the FDA, it will face a regulator that looks quite different than it did in February. Former Commissioner Marty Makary, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) director Vinay Prasad and Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) Acting Director Tracy Beth Høeg have all departed the agency. Prasad reportedly intervened in the initial review of bitopertin, expressing his skepticism about the drug’s efficacy.
If Disc’s drug is cleared for the market, it will join Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals’ Scenesse, a subcutaneous implant that is the only treatment approved for EPP and to prevent phototoxic reactions.
Disc began development of bitopertin in 2021 when the company gained global rights to the asset from Roche. At the time, Disc paid an undisclosed upfront fee for the candidate and offered Roche more than $200 million in potential milestone payments.
Still to come
Beyond bitopertin, BMO is bullish on Disc because of the company’s two other clinical assets.
One of those is a monoclonal antibody called DISC-3405, designed to increase the production of hepcidin—a key regulator of iron entry into circulation—to therapeutically reduce iron levels. The drug, licensed from Mabwell Therapeutics in 2023, is being studied in a Phase 2 trial for polycythemia vera (PV) and a Phase 1b study for sickle cell disease.
In early September, Disc said that DISC-3405 increased hepcidin and lowered serum iron in patients with PV, translating to reduced blood draws and symptom burden, according to a poster presentation at the 2026 Society of Hematologic Oncology meeting.
