Hyundai's Canadian subsidiary has recently confirmed an Elantra N for people who aren't big on contrasting trim. The Monochrome edition brings a more subdued exterior, along with Alcantara for the cabin, forged wheels, and some carbon-fiber exterior components for good measure. Prior to Canada, the special edition was detailed for Australia and the South Korean market.
The Monochrome could reach US dealers later, but all three announcements so far give us no decision to report on. Customers in Canada, meanwhile, can start thinking about which version of the special edition they want. The version question matters a lot because carbon-fiber goodies are optional.
By default, buyers get the black-themed aesthetic and Alcantara interior treatment. The upper version adds mirror caps and a rear spoiler in carbon fiber, which are pretty interesting additions when you remember that no suspension or powertrain changes are in store for this fellow. Monochrome revisits the regular sedan's exterior details, reducing the visual competition between the body and accents.
You can see the form without a separate color drawing an outline around the lower half of the car, and that is particularly different from trying to disguise the N as a rental-spec Elantra. Abyss Black Pearl makes the most literal interpretation, drawing the dark and body details together. Performance Blue offers the more interesting one, so Monochrome doesn't automatically mean black paint.
Hyundai and the N division describe the wheels as newly designed forged items, yet both failed to mention any weight savings. The safe conclusion is to view it as a new design that puts an emphasis on reducing unsprung mass over looks alone. The upper version's carbon-fiber parts add a different material and finish to the mirrors and rear spoiler, yet Hyundai has once again failed to mention any weight savings.
Photo: Hyundai Hopping inside, buyers are treated to a little more than Monochrome-specific Alcantara here and there. Black buttons on the Alcantara-wrapped steering wheel also need highlighting, with Alcantara further appearing on select interior components.
Over in Australia , the Elantra N Monochrome goes by the name i30 N Sedan Monochrome. The i30 moniker also designates the European model, where you get non-N versions of the i30 in hatchback, wagon, and fastback specifications. Just like the i20 N, the i30 N for Europe has been discontinued due to strict emission regulations.
The i30 N Sedan Monochrome will first go on sale in the latter part of October 2026 in South Korea as the Avante N Monochrome, with details for other markets to be published closer to the planned rollout dates. In South Korea, the newcomer will go on sale on October 29. Two days later, it will be displayed at the Hyundai N Festival at the Everland Speedway.
All versions can be had with either a six-speed manual or an eight-speed DCT of the wet-clutch variety. The metric output figures are 280 ps (276 hp) and 40.0 kgfm (392 Nm or 289 lb-ft), with peak torque offered at 2,100 through 4,700 revolutions per minute. When N Grin Shift mode is engaged, the DCT version temporarily reaches 290 ps (286 hp).

Werner Enterprises issued adjusted earnings-per-share guidance of 15 to 16 cents for the third quarter on Monday, which was significantly below the current consensus estimate of 36 cents. The company flagged 18 cents in cumulative cost headwinds from elevated diesel fuel prices, higher driver recruitment and retention expenses, and a reserve adjustment for prior insurance claims.
The company also forecast revenue of $946 million to $951 million for the period, which was only slightly lower than analysts’ expectation for $953.6 million. The news release didn’t provide any update to the company’s prior guidance around tractor counts or pricing.
Werner’s ( NASDAQ: WERN ) prior guidance for the quarter called for a 10% to 13% year-over-year increase in revenue per total mile at its one-way fleet. The metric was 10% higher y/y in the second quarter, with truck utilization improving 16% y/y. The outlook also called for revenue per truck per week at its dedicated fleet (80% of the TL network) to increase by 3% to 5% y/y for the full year.
Truckload fuel surcharges operate on a one-week lag. Diesel prices were up sequentially in nine of the 13 weeks of the third quarter. By month, retail diesel prices dipped 1% sequentially in July, but increased 10% sequentially in August and another 15% in September. The near-term headwind will become an earnings tailwind when prices revert.
J.B. Hunt Transport Services ( NASDAQ: JBHT ) issued a similar warning at an investor conference in mid-September. Its actual third-quarter results , reported last week, came in slightly better than feared. Management from the multimodal transportation provider said it is typical to incur meaningful cost increases in the early part of an upcycle, but that it remains bullish on its ability to price freight above inflation and restore margins.

Werner executives said in August that they were unfazed by the post-July 4 slowdown , chalking it up to a normal seasonal lull heading into peak season. They pointed to the TL industry’s capacity correction, aimed at removing unsafe and non-compliant drivers, as the primary catalyst for the outlook. The supply-side reduction has allowed Werner and other carriers to meaningfully raise rates this year for the first time following a nearly four-year downturn.
Werner said in September that demand among its discount-retail and food-and-beverage customers remained level from the second quarter into the third quarter, and that it was seeing elevated minibid activity at its one-way fleet.
Werner will report third-quarter results on Oct. 27 after the market closes.
Shares of WERN were down 1.1% at 10:21 a.m. EDT on Monday compared to the S&P 500, which was up 0.7%. The stock is off 31% since a mid-July peak.
Why it matters? The update shows the significant cost pressures carriers are currently facing—specifically rising diesel fuel prices and higher driver recruitment and retention expenses. It signals that the industry’s recovery following a multi-year downturn will not be linear, and that while carriers are raising rates, profitability is still being squeezed by early-upcycle cost inflation.

Springer rare earth and gallium deposit. ( Image courtesy of Volta Metals. )
By: Staff Writer October 19, 2026
Volta Metals (CSE: VLTA) has more than doubled the indicated rare earth resource at its Springer project in Ontario, placing it among North America’s five largest by measured and indicated resource tonnage as it advances toward an economic assessment in 2027. Shares surged.
The updated lifted indicated tonnage by 116% to 122.4 million tonnes grading 0.59% total rare earth oxides (TREO). A further 197.5 million tonnes grading 0.53% TREO are classified as inferred. The estimate also includes the project’s first gallium assessment 4,427 tonnes of in-situ gallium within the indicated resource, including a higher-grade zone of 14.8 million tonnes averaging 56 grams per tonne.
“We believe Springer is shaping up as one of the few large, road-accessible sources of magnet rare earths, and potentially gallium, in North America, at a time when the market is paying a premium for supply from outside China,” Volta president and CEO Kerem Usenmez said in a statement.
The expansion comes as Western governments seek to reduce their dependence on China, which dominates global rare earth processing and gallium production. Both commodities are strategically valuable, with rare earths used in permanent magnets for electric vehicles and wind turbines, while gallium is essential to certain semiconductor technologies.
Volta shares jumped 15% to 30¢ apiece on Monday in Toronto, valuing the company at $43.8 million. The stock has traded in a 12-month window of 14¢ to 40¢.
High-grade expansion
Springer’s indicated high-grade core grew 140% to 27.6 million tonnes grading 1% TREO, with an estimated net metal revenue of C$384 ($272) per tonne, equivalent to C$10.6 billion ($7.5 billion) in gross in-situ metal value.
The inferred high-grade core increased ninefold to 26.7 million tonnes grading 0.94% TREO, with an estimated net metal revenue of C$333 per tonne ($236). The zone remains open for expansion.
Gallium could provide an additional revenue stream, although Volta has yet to establish whether the metal can be economically recovered. The company is conducting metallurgical studies to assess recovery methods and potential commercial viability.
Magnet rare earths — neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium — account for about 22.4% of the indicated resource’s total rare earth oxide content, a proportion Volta says is among the highest in North America.
North American rare earth projects ranked by measured and indicated tonnage, including reserves where reported. Inferred tonnage is shown separately for context and is not used in the ranking. (S&P Global Market Intelligence database, May 2025; Springer at the Sept. 30, 2026 MRE.)
Springer ranks fifth among North American rare earth projects by combined measured and indicated resource tonnage, Volta said, citing S&P Global Market Intelligence data.
However, the ranking measures resource size rather than economic potential and does not account for differences in grade, metallurgy, development costs or project maturity.
Development outlook
Located about 70 km east of Sudbury, Springer benefits from direct highway access , on-site power and nearby natural gas and rail infrastructure. The deposit’s low strip ratio could also support future mine development, although the project’s economics remain untested.
Volta plans additional drilling to expand and refine the resource while advancing metallurgical work on rare earth and gallium recovery.
The company is targeting a preliminary economic assessment (PEA) in the first half of 2027, which would provide an initial evaluation of potential mining costs, processing requirements and project economics.

The U.S. Department of Transportation announced $200 million in grants for 14 truck parking projects in 12 states. The funding will add or expand parking along major highways, near ports , and at a Texas border crossing, with improvements to lighting, security , and parking availability information.
What’s Related
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the awards last week. The department says 40% of truckers spend more than an hour a day searching for parking, and the grants aim to give drivers safer alternatives to highway shoulders and ramps.
“They shouldn’t have to spend over an hour looking for a safe place to rest at the end of the day,” Duffy said.
RELATED STORIES: Ranking the Lower 48 States by Truck Parking Availability | The 10 U.S. Cities Where Trucks Park on Ramps Most Often
Where the money is going
The grants cover new parking facilities and expansions at existing stops. Projects include:
Tennessee: Nearly $24 million for approximately 500 spaces at five Pilot Travel Centers along I-40 and I-24 near Nashville and Knoxville.
Georgia: $11.95 million for approximately 275 public truck spaces near the Port of Savannah in Garden City.
North Carolina: About $6 million for approximately 140 truck spaces and 50 container staging positions at the Port of Wilmington.
Texas: About $9.2 million for a project providing access to a new 305-space facility near the Los Indios Port of Entry, plus about $5.1 million for about 100 spaces at a Pilot Travel Center in Fort Worth.
Connecticut: $13.5 million for up to 260 spaces along I-91 in Enfield, with bathrooms, vending areas, and parking availability monitoring.
Iowa: Approximately $24.5 million to expand and modernize six public rest areas along I-80.
Wisconsin: $15 million to add approximately 106 spaces at two rest areas along I-41 in Dodge County.
“This investment will deliver hundreds of new spots across the country, helping hardworking truck drivers get the rest they need and reducing dangerous roadside parking on some of America’s most important corridors,” said Derek D. Barrs, administrator of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration.
Other awards will fund projects in Arkansas, California, Illinois, Minnesota, and Nebraska. Minnesota’s project will replace a rest area near Fergus Falls that closed due to recurring flooding, adding about 63 truck spaces along I-94.
Other DOT news
The parking grants follow several other DOT announcements this year involving freight data , truck driver qualifications, and fuel deliveries :
Sharing freight data: The DOT announced the American Supply Chain Sovereignty Initiative , proposing a dashboard that connects ports , ocean carriers, trucking companies, railroads and retailers to help reduce cargo delays.
Stepping up enforcement: The department said its trucking safety crackdown removed more than 11,500 truck drivers from service and shut down 7,500 commercial driver’s license training schools.
Removing training providers: Federal regulators removed more than 110 truck driver training schools from the training registry and put more than 160 others on notice over training failures and links to English-language violations.
Easing fuel delivery rules: A 90-day waiver temporarily eased hours-of-service rules for gasoline and diesel shipments , with required rest breaks and restrictions on which carriers could participate.

This article draws on lessons from the first triennium of PSE&G’s Energy Efficiency (EE) program and how those experiences have helped shape our approach as the program has progressed. Intended for energy companies, industry peers and others involved in shaping or advancing energy efficiency efforts, the article shares insights on program management and delivery, customer engagement, partnerships, workforce development and other considerations involved in implementing energy efficiency programs at scale.
New Jersey enacted the Clean Energy Act in 2018, followed by an Energy Master Plan in 2019 that set goals addressing the production, distribution, consumption and conservation of energy across the state. This policy set the stage for the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (NJBPU) to issue the Clean Energy Future—Energy Efficiency (CEF-EE) framework, which required all New Jersey utilities to submit filings for energy efficiency programs to help the state meet its goals.
COMMENTARY
Launched in 2020, PSE&G’s Clean Energy Future—Energy Efficiency I program represented one of the state’s most significant investments in energy efficiency, electric vehicle infrastructure, and clean energy workforce development. Over its first three years, the initiative offered a clear view into what large-scale clean energy implementation looks like in practice, and generated lessons that continue to inform the program as it evolves.
The program’s first triennium had measurable impact, reaching more than 440,000 customers whose participation collectively reduced electricity use by approximately 2.6 million megawatt-hours of electricity, enough to power nearly 380,000 homes. Natural gas customers are expected to continue saving more than 69 million therms per year, while overall customer savings were projected to reach $678 million annually. Those outcomes translate into avoided emissions of roughly 1.9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year. Beyond the numbers, our program’s story is also about people. Through the sponsored Clean Energy Jobs Program, PSE&G and its partners supported the placement of more than 2,700 New Jersey residents into clean energy careers, reinforcing how workforce development can expand access to opportunity while building the talent needed to support the state’s skilled workforce.
PSE&G Clean Energy Future—Energy Efficiency program has played an important role in advancing energy efficiency across the state and supporting New Jersey’s position as a national leader in energy efficiency. The state is now ranked #8 in the country on the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (ACEEE) state scorecard , up from #14 in 2022 . Building on these early results, the utility entered the second triennium of its energy efficiency program in January 2025, and lessons from the first triennium continue to inform how we approach program delivery and customer engagement today.
While the utility has always offered energy efficiency programs, the scale of the CEF-EE program was unprecedented. To achieve these outcomes during the first triennium, the program required significant organizational buildout. The utility established a Clean Energy Solutions group to develop the infrastructure, staffing, and processes needed to support the investment and meet state-mandated energy efficiency goals. This involved creating new specialized, customer-centric teams, designing strategies to engage and increase participation for both residential and business customers, and building the operational systems necessary to manage the program consistently and effectively across the utility as it scaled. Across these efforts, one principle became increasingly clear: successful program delivery depends on keeping the customer at the center as programs grow in scale and complexity.
Several lessons that emerged during the first triennium have continued to prove relevant as PSE&G’s energy efficiency portfolio has evolved, including the importance of building the organizational structure needed to manage programs at scale, engaging customers in ways that reflect their different needs and barriers, developing strong delivery and community partnerships, and investing in the capabilities needed to support continued growth. As the portfolio continues to evolve, these lessons remain central to how we approach program delivery and growth.
Building the Program Management Structure to Scale Energy Efficiency
Soon after the program launched and participation grew, PSE&G established a Project Management Organization (PMO) to support the scale and complexity of the portfolio. The PMO streamlined swim lanes for measurement, forecasting and reporting, allowing operational teams to focus on day-to-day program delivery. This structure strengthened oversight of program performance, improved tracking of investment expenses and energy savings, and enhanced coordination with contractors and vendors, including management of contractor relationships and oversight of vendor operations. Together, these changes positioned the portfolio to scale effectively.
We also learned that strong feedback loops and flexible processes are critical as programs grow in scale and complexity. This is especially important when engaging the wide range of internal and external stakeholders that are essential to successful program delivery.
Trade allies, implementation vendors, contractors, and suppliers are the customer-facing drivers of this work and essential to program execution. Early in the implementation phase, it became clear that the scale and complexity of the portfolio required stronger and more consistent quality oversight for partners across all program lines.
To support this, we strengthened our existing processes and assigned dedicated Quality Assurance / Quality Control (QAQC) resources to help manage the growing number of trade allies and vendors. This approach ensured that partners were screened against clear criteria and held accountable to program standards throughout their engagement. These improvements reinforced program integrity, supported a consistent customer experience, and positioned the portfolio for long-term growth.
As the program scaled, we refined our approach to working with implementation partners and recognized the importance of engaging stakeholders across the energy supply chain. Manufacturers, distributors, contractors and technology providers played important roles in driving adoption across both the residential and business portfolios. Our experience reinforced a broader lesson that remains relevant today: effective engagement across the supply chain requires clear messaging and incentives, including:
Incentives for manufacturers to produce higher-efficiency equipment.
Awareness campaigns for distributors to stock high-efficiency products.
Incentives for contractors to promote efficient solutions.
We also found that customer experience cannot be separated from program delivery. Integrating customer touchpoints, including technical service calls, meter installations and customer service interactions, creates opportunities to raise program awareness, make it easier for customers to connect with relevant offerings and deepen our role as a trusted energy advisor.
Managing program transitions and maintaining continuity also proved important. The first three-year cycle included two formal extensions that aligned the portfolio with the statewide regulatory cycle and supported planning for the next triennium. As we prepared to move from one program cycle to the next, changes to program requirements required updates across implementation, marketing and other areas of program delivery. During this transition, certain marketing and implementation activities were paused while those changes were incorporated into the next phase of the program, affecting the pacing of work across internal teams, vendors, delivery partners and the broader network.
The experience reinforced the importance of ongoing communication and coordination with regulatory stakeholders, internal teams and delivery partners throughout the transition. It also highlighted the need for sufficient time to translate program changes into implementation and ensure those involved in delivering and communicating the programs understand what is changing. Managing these transitions deliberately can help maintain as much consistency as possible for customers, partners and the broader market.
Fostering Trust with Residential Customers Through Partnerships and Targeted Outreach
One of the most persistent challenges in implementing energy efficiency programs is driving awareness and building trust, particularly in low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. While a full suite of offerings, including energy-saving appliance rebates and discounts, on-bill-repayment, and home energy assessments was available to all customers within our service territory, we found that tailoring opportunities for specific customer groups, especially LMI households, was important to achieving broad participation and better addressing customers’ energy needs.
Many customers questioned why a utility would help reduce consumption of its own product, and offerings that included no-cost services or significant incentives were sometimes met with skepticism. To address this perception, we partnered with trusted organizations, such as state agencies, municipalities, community partners, and payment assistance programs that customers already interacted with. These partnerships increased credibility and improved participation.
Market segmentation also proved critical. Different communities faced unique barriers, so we implemented tailored engagement strategies and incentive structures for both low-income customers and moderate-income customers (250–400% of federal poverty level). Data-driven targeting, informed by marketing research and focus groups, revealed valuable insights about effective messaging and imagery, allowing us to deliver more resonant communications. And by analyzing usage patterns and demographics, we proactively engaged customers with relevant offerings rather than relying on broad awareness campaigns that proved less effective.
Employee ambassadorship was another important factor to program success. Staff across departments—from meter installers to customer service representatives—were trained to communicate program benefits using simple, consistent messaging. For multifamily properties, we developed streamlined processes to address challenges such as complex ownership structures and split incentives, removing common participation barriers.
Continuous improvement also shaped our residential offerings. We merged initial quick home energy checks with comprehensive home performance assessments to streamline the customer journey, making it easier for them to receive immediate energy-saving measures, along with evaluations for deeper energy efficiency improvements during a single home visit.
On-bill repayment (OBR) mechanisms at 0% interest over five-year repayment periods further reduced barriers, eliminating upfront costs and simplifying repayment through the utility bill. This experience reinforced the importance of accessible payment options in reducing barriers to participation.
As a result of these efforts, during the first triennium we completed nearly 90,000 home energy assessments, issued rebates for more than 124,000 energy-efficient appliances, enabled the recycling of over 23,000 appliances and the purchase of nearly 335,000 smart thermostats through our PSE&G Marketplace platform. By the end of the triennium, more than 440,000 customers had participated in our energy efficiency programs.
As implementation has continued, advanced technologies have expanded opportunities for customer engagement beyond traditional energy efficiency upgrades. Solutions such as smart thermostats, efficient heat pump systems and AI-driven energy management platforms offer new opportunities for savings and comfort across customer groups. These technologies are also expanding the ways customers can engage with and manage their energy use, reinforcing the broader lesson that effective programs must continue to adapt to changing customer needs and available technologies.
Driving Business Customer Engagement, Adoption and Impact
In large-scale energy efficiency programs, distinguishing between residential and business customers is not enough. Business customers themselves have different needs, barriers and decision-making processes that require more tailored approaches. Through our work, we learned that tailoring programs to specific business segments significantly improved participation compared to broad marketing efforts. A comprehensive “end-to-end” approach combining opportunity assessments, cost-benefit analysis, implementation support and payment options helped business customers better understand program benefits and move forward with participation.
For larger commercial customers, self-service web tools proved insufficient. So, we created a dedicated support model working with our key customer advisors and a newly developed business development team. This approach enabled our representatives to understand each business’s core operations, budget constraints, and strategic objectives before recommending tailored energy efficiency solutions.
Engagement timelines also varied dramatically by segment: large commercial projects often required three to five years from initial contact to completion, while small business projects could typically be completed in four to six months. This divergence reinforced the need for distinct engagement strategies. Our small business program employed a turnkey approach, providing assessments and connecting participants directly with trade allies to streamline implementation.
Case studies and real-world success stories emerged as effective tools for building customer buy-in, particularly when they demonstrated benefits beyond energy savings, such as operational improvements, increased comfort and reduced maintenance costs. Implementation partners also proved critical, serving as trusted messengers in the small business community. Equipping these partners with clear tools, processes, and support materials significantly strengthened their ability to extend program outreach and drive adoption.
These efforts engaged more than 16,000 businesses across sectors ranging from small shops and manufacturing facilities to hospitals, corporate offices, schools and universities, including nearly 1,400 small businesses. They also led to the completion of more than 25,000 commercial and industrial projects statewide.
Investing in a Clean Energy Workforce to Meet Growing Demand
Implementing energy efficiency programs at scale requires not only strong program infrastructure and customer engagement, but also a skilled workforce to deliver the work. As demand for clean energy jobs grew, workforce development became an important component of PSE&G’s energy efficiency efforts. Established in 2020, the PSE&G-sponsored Clean Energy Jobs Program was designed to help build that pipeline while creating opportunities for New Jersey residents. During the first triennium alone, the program helped place 2,700 New Jersey residents into clean energy careers.
A steering committee made up of community organizations and strategic hiring and recruiting partners played an important role in the program’s approach. This public-private partnership helped connect candidates with job and career advancement opportunities while raising awareness of available employment and training through various outreach channels.
The program also addressed barriers to entering and succeeding in clean energy careers. On-the-job training provided a pathway into the sector, while wraparound services, such as childcare and transportation assistance, helped broaden the candidate pool and support training completion. Participants received interpersonal skills training, along with guidance and feedback from program leads and mentors. During the first triennium, the Clean Energy Jobs Program also provided access to Building Performance Institute (BPI) certification for 600 PSE&G job supplier and subcontractor employees already working in clean energy roles, strengthening the capabilities of the existing workforce.
Applying Early Lessons to Continued Progress
Our second triennium , launched in January 2025, built on the residential and business energy efficiency offerings established during the first triennium while expanding the portfolio to include building decarbonization and demand response.
The results since the program’s inception demonstrate the continued impact of these investments. Nearly 525,000 residential and business customers have participated in our energy efficiency programs, with that participation generating more than $1 billion in annual customer savings. We have also delivered approximately $1.1 billion in customer rebates and incentives to help make energy efficiency improvements more affordable. In addition, we have completed more than 111,000 home energy assessments and enrolled more than 37,600 customers in demand response programs.
Business customers have benefited from these investments as well. Approximately 22,500 businesses have participated in our energy efficiency programs, including more than 2,200 small businesses. Those small business participants are realizing approximately $31 million in annual energy savings. Additionally, nearly 36,000 commercial and industrial projects have been completed statewide through a network of more than 1,000 trade allies, including union partners who are helping delivery and implement energy efficiency improvement projects across our service territory.
Collectively, these programs have generated approximately 3.4 million megawatt-hours (MWh) of annual electricity savings, enough to power more than 497,000 homes for one year. Gas savings are delivering approximately 87 million therms annually, equal to taking more than 550,000 gasoline-powered cars off the road. Together, these savings are helping to avoid approximately 2.5 million metric tons of carbon emissions annually.
Our approach to customer experience has also evolved. Bringing our Customer Care and Clean Energy Solutions teams together under one leadership structure is helping streamline processes, improve efficiency and deepen customer relationships.
Workforce development has continued to support program delivery as well. As of June 2026, our Clean Energy Jobs Program had supported the placement of more than 11,000 New Jersey residents into clean energy careers. We are also strengthening the program through expanded contractor training for emerging technologies, including high-efficiency heat pumps.
Beyond these workforce efforts, we are exploring additional technologies and approaches through the broader energy efficiency portfolio, including pilots involving geothermal systems and virtual power plant models. As our programs grow and change, we remain focused on meeting customer needs and identifying new ways to deliver energy savings and value.
Recommendations for Success
Based on our experience implementing a large-scale utility energy efficiency portfolio, several factors have been important to successful program delivery:
Build organizational structures that can support program growth , including dedicated measurement, forecasting and quality control functions.
Keep the customer at the center of program design and delivery , with a focus on making programs easier to understand, access and navigate.
Tailor engagement to different customer needs , using data and market insights, trusted community partnerships and relevant examples to reach residential and business customer segments more effectively.
Build strong trade ally and implementation partner networks , with the training, support and quality standards needed for consistent program delivery.
Maintain strong regulatory collaboration and manage program transitions deliberately , with ongoing communication and coordination among regulatory stakeholders, internal teams, vendors and delivery partners.
Invest in workforce development , building both the talent pipeline and the skills needed to support program delivery and new technologies.
— Lauren Thomas is vice president, Clean Energy Solutions—Customer Solutions at PSE&G.

U.S. Army Sgt. Jeffrey Davis, an electronic warfare specialist with the 3rd Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 25th Infantry Division, operates a dismounted spectrum awareness system during Exercise Lightning Surge 1 at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii, Jan. 22, 2026. The system provides real-time situational awareness of the electromagnetic spectrum, feeding critical data into the Army's Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) ecosystem for commanders to make more informed decisions. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Duke Edwards)
WASHINGTON — When the Army for the first time attempted to integrate Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) tech from defense firm Anduril into its existing comms systems, not everything went exactly to plan, Army and company officials revealed to Breaking Defense this week.
“It wasn’t seamless, and we and we learned a lot,” Brig. Gen. Shane Taylor, Portfolio Management Executive for Command and Control Information Network (C2IN), said on the sidelines of the annual AUSA conference this week. “There’s always growing point pains in these. I just think that a lot of the things that we saw out there were normal, like all right, we’re putting … a group that hasn’t necessarily worked together, so it’s just that normal growing pains with that.”
The test had come in September, when the Army’s 25th Infantry Division attempted to use Anduril’s Lattice platform during Lightning Surge 5 in Hawaii, which the Army described as a “multi-phase campaign to modernize its command-and-control architecture.” Up until then, Anduril’s NGC2 tech had been used by the 4th ID in Colorado where it was paired with new, mostly commercial hardware and software.
Lockheed Martin, which is leading the integration on the 25th ID’s portion of the NGC2 architecture , served as the integrator for Anduril’s platform. Chandra Marshall, vice president of multi-domain combat solutions at the defense giant, told Breaking Defense the company expected “it would be a challenge.”
“I would say outside of Lockheed Martin, yes, I think some people are surprised at how much of a challenge it has been,” Marshall said in an interview at the AUSA conference.
She explained scaling with Lattice was an issue passing data through the system “just is not at the state it should be right now with bringing in the Lattice product.”
An Anduril official, for his part, acknowledged the growing pains, but noted that they discovered technical limitations with the communications architecture writ large.
“It was our first time with a host of technologies at the 25th [ID],” James Craven, Program Manager for NGC2 for Anduril, said in an interview Wednesday. “Working on TSM radios that were not the same waveform or configuration that we had used at 4th ID, and [Lightning Surge] was also several novel mission threads as well.”
Getting Lattice and the older comms structure on the same page will be key to the Army’s NGC2 efforts, as Army and industry officials noted that the 25th ID’s architecture is largely representative of what they’ll have to build on top of as they begin to baseline and field other units within I Corps throughout the upcoming fiscal year.
“The major difference between the 4th Infantry Division and the 25th, is that [25th] will continue to preserve some legacy capabilities … and we’re going to make sure that that we maintain seamless integrations with legacy equipment because not everybody’s going to get a fresh fielding like the 4th Infantry Division,” Craven said.
Lockheed’s Marshall said that for its part, the company is making sure the 25th ID gets “back to working operational architecture so that we can continue to build on the capabilities.”
New Environment, Different Technology
Part of the challenge, Army and company officials said, was also just the vastly different environment the tech was called to operate in and on what mobile platforms.
For example, Fort Carson, Colo., where 4th ID is based, is a much more open, plain environment as opposed to the dense jungle in Hawaii with 25th ID. Moreover, 4th ID is a heavier unit, with soldiers operating out of Strykers, while 25th ID’s primary platforms are lighter Infantry Squad Vehicles.
“We don’t have the same type of permissiveness from putting equipment on platforms perspective that we do with like Stryker brigades,” Joseph Welch, the Army’s portfolio acquisition executive for Command and Control (C2) and Counter C2, said in an interview at AUSA. “We’ve had to work through what does that really mean for a mobile infantry unit in terms of what types of transport solutions and what type of compute capacity we can put at echelon. … There’s probably some additional tweaks and optimizations we’re going to make that’s based on just the reality of the formation type.”
As for working with other legacy tech, Cravens said Anduril has been partnering with radio providers, C2IN and 25th ID to on the operational configurations such as how big the channels are, how to separate data from voice channels on radios, how to ensure the appropriate soldiers within a unit have beyond line of sight communications such as Starshield , all in order to provide a “fight tonight” capability for the data layer.
One of the key lessons at Lightning Surge 5, Craven said, was filling the request to go smaller on things like edge computing capabilities. While they integrated Lattice onto the Mounted Family of Computer Systems at 4th ID, last month was the first time they did it on tablets.
However, that integration was requested and done in the middle of the exercise, Craven said, hoping that next time, they’ll have a chance to work that integration before they get out to the field.
Outfitting More Divisions With NGC2
Following the decision to field I Corps with the NGC2 architecture and associated capabilities, the Army is in the process of providing the corps headquarters capabilities and applications while looking to baseline the other divisions.
Taylor echoed the idea that 25th ID is an important first step in that journey given a more representative approach to how the Army will have to field given many of the other formations are closer to them having not received any equipment.
“I think the 25th one was very helpful because those ITN divisions, when we come in with the Next Gen C2 capabilities, that’s the integration that we’re going to do,” he said.
Though, Welch said they’ll continue to upgrade 4th ID with some “burn down items” that came out of Project Convergence over the summer, they need to address in terms of systems to bring forward or leave behind.
Welch noted that the importance of testing over the past year with the ITN equipment in 25th has helped ensure the baseline is solid and they have good configurations.
While there is no definitive timeline in terms of when the other divisions under I Corps will get baselined, Welch said it will occur within the fiscal year. The continuing resolution is having some impact on that, he said, acknowledging they’ll have to look at “pacing” some systems.
Additionally, there are logistics the Army will have to take into consideration in terms of moving systems forward to the divisions, with units spanning up to Alaska and in the Pacific.
Overall, they’re trying to not overwhelm these units with new capabilities.
“We are trying not to have NGC2 coming in there as a disruptor to their mission focus, but as an enabler of it. As you know, NGC2 is a multi-layered stack capability. So our teams are in routine communications for the planning aspect of when we’re going to start introducing those,” he said. “It’s really more aligned to the opportunities that we have when we try to align to their exercises and their training.”

American Electric Power (AEP) and X-energy have agreed to evaluate a 960-MW small modular reactor (SMR) project in Indiana, backed by Amazon development funding and a proposed long-term power purchase agreement designed to protect existing utility customers from project costs. The 12-reactor project would be the second deployment under Amazon and X-energy’s collaboration to develop more than 5 GW of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.
AEP and X-energy announced the joint development agreement (JDA) on Oct. 19, identifying the retired Breed Generating Station in Sullivan County, Indiana, as a potential location for 12 of X-energy’s 80-MW Xe-100 reactors. The proposed plant would be configured in three groups of four reactors, each totaling 320 MW, for a combined 960 MW.
The companies are evaluating an AEP-owned brownfield site at or near Indiana Michigan Power’s (I&M’s) former coal-fired Breed station. According to AEP , the plant would proceed to construction only if the development reaches a final investment decision (FID). If built, it would supply electricity to the regional grid and could operate for more than 60 years.
Amazon will provide development funding and intends to purchase the plant’s electricity under a long-term contract. AEP said the agreement would cover the costs of the facility and its operations for the contract’s duration, an arrangement intended to protect existing utility customers from the financial risks of developing new nuclear capacity.
“Our agreements with Amazon and X-energy will provide all necessary capital protections and financial safeguards that we have said are essential for any potential nuclear project to move forward,” AEP Chairman, President and CEO Bill Fehrman said in the announcement.
The development follows two other major customer-linked generation announcements by AEP. On Oct. 14, the utility announced plans to invest approximately $4 billion in a 702-MW Bloom Energy fuel cell development in Wyoming to supply Google under a 20-year agreement. On Oct. 13, Mainspring Energy announced an agreement to supply AEP up to 1.6 GW of linear generators through 2034.
The Indiana plant would also represent the second project under Amazon and X-energy’s nuclear collaboration, following Energy Northwest’s Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. As POWER reported in October 2025 , Cascade’s full build-out envisions 12 Xe-100 reactors totaling 960 MW, beginning with a 320-MW, four-reactor block.
Amazon’s Nuclear Investment Strategy Takes Shape in Indiana
The proposed Indiana project builds on an investment relationship between Amazon and X-energy that began in 2024, when Amazon led the reactor developer’s Series C-1 financing round through its $2 billion Climate Pledge Fund. According to Amazon’s Oct. 19 announcement , the financing round ultimately closed at $700 million, supporting completion of X-energy’s reactor design and licensing activities and the first phase of its TRISO-X nuclear fuel fabrication facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
That investment accompanied a broader collaboration targeting more than 5 GW of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039. Amazon is now supporting individual developments through project funding and commitments to purchase electricity.
At Cascade, Amazon agreed to fund initial feasibility work and secured rights to purchase electricity from the first 320-MW block. The Indiana proposal follows a similar commercial approach, although Amazon’s stated intent to purchase electricity covers the proposed 960-MW facility.
X-energy said Amazon’s contribution to the Indiana development would be milestone-based. Amazon, meanwhile, said it would serve as the plant’s first electricity customer, purchasing output once the facility becomes operational. The company expects the nuclear capacity to serve both the regional grid and its expanding data center operations.
“Together, we’re looking to develop nearly a gigawatt of carbon-free power for the regional grid and pay our full costs without passing them to others,” Josh Weissman, Amazon’s vice president of Data Center Infrastructure Capacity Delivery, said on Oct. 19.
Amazon also linked the proposed nuclear development to its participation in the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which the company committed to paying the full electricity costs of serving its data centers, including additional infrastructure needed to accommodate their demand.
AEP would contribute nuclear operating experience through I&M, which operates the 2,278-MW Donald C. Cook Nuclear Plant in Michigan. I&M’s 2024 integrated resource plan selected subsequent license renewal for both Cook units.
X-energy’s Xe-100 Technology and Commercial Development
The Xe-100 is an 80-MW high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) that uses helium as its coolant and tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) particle fuel. The fuel consists of uranium particles encapsulated within multiple protective ceramic layers engineered to retain fission products at high temperatures. X-energy emphasizes the reactor’s passive safety characteristics and compact footprint, which it says support deployment at industrial facilities and existing power generation sites.
Amazon also highlighted the technology’s cooling flexibility. According to the company, Xe-100 plants can use air-cooled condensers, water-cooled systems, or hybrid cooling configurations depending on local conditions and available water resources.
X-energy said the Indiana proposal is its third announced commercial Xe-100 project in the U.S. and fourth worldwide, part of an approximately 11.5-GW commercial pipeline. Its first planned U.S. deployment is a four-reactor project at Dow’s Seadrift manufacturing complex on the Texas Gulf Coast, which is designed to supply both electricity and high-temperature industrial steam. According to X-energy, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is in the final stages of reviewing the project’s construction permit application.
For now, the Indiana development remains at the feasibility stage. The companies have not disclosed the proposed plant’s capital cost, Amazon’s development funding commitment, the term or price of the planned electricity contract, or the eventual ownership structure. They also have not announced an FID date, construction schedule, commercial operation target, or NRC licensing pathway.

Businesses spend an estimated $1.54 million a year on manual procurement and supply chain work that AI could automate , according to a new Ivalua report. Yet just 34% of organizations surveyed have put AI into production in procurement.
What’s Related
The report found that 86% of organizations are deploying, piloting, or considering AI in procurement. Among organizations already using AI, 69% said they have seen a return on their investment.
The findings also show the way teams spend their time is changing. Some 72% of AI adopters said the technology has increased the time available for strategy and building supplier relationships.
RELATED STORIES: AI Is Reshaping Procurement Jobs, But Few Leaders Have Changed Them | Why Procurement Teams Need Rules Before Giving AI More Power
The cost of waiting
The dollar figure comes from two survey findings: average annual spending of $8.29 million on procurement and supply chain staff, and an average of 18.6% of team time spent on manual tasks respondents said could be automated or handled by AI. Multiplying those figures produces an estimated annual labor cost of approximately $1.54 million per organization.
That calculation estimates the staff time spent on those tasks. It does not measure cash savings companies have achieved by introducing AI, and the amount each organization could save would depend on its staffing costs and the work it automates.
“The cost of waiting is becoming harder to ignore,” said Paul Zammit, AI GTM Lead at Ivalua. “Organizations that have taken AI into production are already seeing returns, while those stuck in pilot mode are paying twice: millions spent on manual work, and strategic ground conceded to faster-moving competitors.”
Data problems slow adoption
Half of respondents said their procurement data is not reliable enough to produce meaningful AI insights. Nearly half (45%) said information sits in four or more separate systems, making it harder to build a complete picture of purchasing and suppliers.
Meanwhile, 51% of procurement leaders said their teams trail other business functions in AI adoption. Sapio Research conducted the survey in March 2026, including 800 procurement decision-makers and 200 CIOs, evenly split across four countries.
“The organizations seeing the greatest gains aren't simply those investing in AI, but those putting the right data foundations in place to make it useful,” Zammit said.

source_document.body:
Construction of the open pit at Penco in Chile. Credit: Aclara Resources
Posted By: Blair McBride October 19, 2026
An updated preliminary economic assessment (PEA) for Aclara Resources’ (TSX: ARA) Penco Module rare earths project in Chile almost doubles its post-tax net present value over a 2021 study despite a doubling in initial capital costs. Shares rose.
Penco’s NPV is now estimated at $344 million, compared with pre-production costs of $244 million, Aclara said Monday. The updated NPV uses an 8% discount rate, compared with 5% in the 2021 study, while the update raises life for the open pit mine by three years to 17 years and the internal rate of return by three percentage points to 26.1%.
Aclara attributes the higher NPV partly to a 55% increase in material processed to 30.8 million tonnes, as well as higher forecast rare earth prices. Penco is about 430 km south of Santiago.
“The Penco Module stands out for its significant heavy rare earth content, particularly dysprosium, terbium and yttrium, and its strategic location in one of Chile’s leading industrial regions,” Aclara CEO Hugh Broadhurst said in a release on Monday.
“Looking ahead, the potential integration of Penco with our separation and metals and alloys facilities in Louisiana offers a compelling opportunity to capture synergies across the value chain and strengthen Aclara’s position as a vertically integrated supplier of critical rare earth materials to global markets.”
Developing supply chain
The updated PEA advances Aclara’s plans to establish an integrated rare earth supply chain in the Americas, linking its South American deposits with processing and manufacturing facilities in the United States. Its Dynamo plant in Louisiana, where construction is targeted to begin in early 2027, would process rare earths mined at Penco and Carina Module in Brazil, currently in the permitting stage. Both sites host rare earths in relatively shallow ionic clays which require no blasting, crushing or grinding to mine.
The Export-Import Bank of the U.S. could provide up to $750 million towards Dynamo’s construction , subject to various coFnditions, the company announced in September. Aclara also operates a rare earth separation demonstration plant in Virginia, where it expects to produce its first separated heavy rare earths in this year’s fourth quarter.
Shares in Aclara gained 3% to $2.97 apiece mid-day Monday, valuing the company at about $736.6 million. The stock has traded in a 12-month range of $2.01 to $5.40.
‘Super pure carbonate’
Though average annual production is forecast to fall about 5% from the 2021 PEA to 732 tonnes of rare earth oxides, Aclara said the new output would include a “super pure rare earth carbonate” comprising such heavy rare earths as dysprosium at 6%, terbium at 0.8%, yttrium at 54.5% and gadolinium at 4.2%.
The new study includes an updated resource of 35.8 million measured and indicated tonnes grading 2,095 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO) for 75,025 contained tonnes TREO, a 19% rise in contained rare earths. Inferred resources grew 29% to 2.2 million tonnes at 1,768 ppm TREO for 3,848 contained tonnes, a 14% rise.
Aclara received its final environmental approval for Penco in June , ending a process that lasted more than four years. It plans to complete a feasibility study for Penco in the first quarter of 2027. Construction of the mine is expected to be finished in 2028.

Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have revealed a further redesign to the Gemini Cooperation’s Asia-Mediterranean network which will see a reorganisation of the regional hub-and-spoke model.
Slated for introduction over the course of the second half of November, the move comes as the two carriers eye a full resumption of Suez transits by early next year, according to Hapag-Lloyd chief executive Rolf Habben Jansen.
“We have announced a fair number of services that already have returned, and some more are returning in the weeks to come,” he said in a press beefing last week.
“As we have said all along, if we go back, we will do it step by step and in a managed way. I’m really happy that’s what we’ve done, because we can also manage the load on the hubs and on the ports in Europe and the Mediterranean.
“So far, that has not caused too many problems, it’s been going well – if there is no change, I would expect that more or less all of our services will be back through Suez, maybe with one or two exceptions, somewhere in the course of Q1 next year,” he added.
The chief development in the revamped network is that Gemini will launch a new “transhipment hub-only” service between China and the west Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, dubbed AE18 by Maersk and SE5 by Hapag-Lloyd, featuring the following port rotation: Shanghai-Xiamen-Tanjung Pelepas-Algeciras-Tangier-Algeciras-Xiamen.
The first vessel on the AE18/SE5 will be the 13,100 teu Maersk Edirne departure from Shanghai on 22 November. The vessel is currently completing her deployment on Maersk’s standalone Asia-Mexico AC2 service.
Maersk said the new service was designed to complement its other Asia-Europe strings as well as flows from Asia to West Africa and South America with its west Mediterranean hubs taking on more relay transhipment responsibilities.
“These changes include the introduction of the new AE18 service, which, together with AE19, will consolidate our existing West Mediterranean hub coverage.
“Through our modular network concept, this will also enable product enhancements for our customers, eg shipping from Asia to West Africa and to the East Coast of Latin America,” it said in a customer advisory.
As a result, Gemini’s Asia-North Europe Loop 1 (Maersk AE2/Hapag NE1) will replace its current first European port of call of Tangier with Rotterdam, “providing an alternative and improved service from Ningbo and Shanghai to Rotterdam”.
The Asia-Mediterranean Loop2 (Maersk AE11/Hapag SE2) will also drop a call at westbound Tangier in favour of Port Said and introduce a pre-Suez call at Salalah.
Meanwhile, the recently inaugurated Asia-Mediterranean Loop4 will insert an additional call at Damietta, close to Port Said and where Gemini appears to be developing a twin-hub strategy, as well as replacing Shanghai with Nansha.
Further to which, the phased approach of returning Gemini services through Suez has been praised by liner analyst Lars Jensen, speaking at the same press briefing as Mr Habben Jansen.
“For me, it has been a very positive surprise so far, that the changeover is happening as slowly as and gradually as it is actually doing,” said Mr Jensen.
“Before the normalization started, my key hypothesis was that this would happen a lot faster, and I’m positively surprised at the restraint we see from the carriers in terms of not making it a fast transition.
“The latest numbers, at least I have, is we are roughly 30%-35% normalised across the market for the Suez routing – slightly more on the backhaul, slightly less on the head haul,” he added.

source_document.body:
PERTH, Australia — To protect a whole continent, Australia has only a regiment’s worth of NASAMS short-range air defense systems. Recognizing this is not nearly enough, Canberra has launched a formal tender for a medium-range, ground-based air defense solution for the Australian Army.
The Department of Defence launched an industry solicitation for the project, christened Project Land 6504, on Oct. 13. The potential deal has already attracted interest globally, with vendors from Europe, Israel, South Korea, Turkey and the United States eying the requirement Down Under.
A primary motivation for filling the gaping hole in Australian defenses is China’s rising military prowess. Alarming many, the People’s Liberation Army sent a naval task group to circumnavigate Australia in early 2025, and then China fired an intercontinental ballistic missile into the South Pacific in July this year.
With China possessing the world’s most diverse missile arsenal, Australia knows it needs better defenses. Land 6504 is therefore looking for a defensive system capable of shooting down ballistic missiles in their terminal phase of flight, as well as address subsonic air-breathing threats.
The National Defence Strategy 2026 prioritized missile defense, calling for “accelerated introduction of medium-range, ground-based, active missile defense through investment in missile launchers and munitions and integrating them with the Australian Defence Force’s command-and-control systems.”
This envisioned off-the-shelf system is expected to be a “proven capability,” contributing to a national, integrated system, the solicitation reads.
South Korea's Hanwha advertised its L-SAM air defense system at the Land Forces 2026 exhibition in Perth, Australia, in early October 2026. (Gordon Arthur)
Money is a perennial problem, however, as AUKUS nuclear-powered submarines soak up available defense funds.
But perhaps the greatest risk is the lightning speed at which this Australian project is moving. Final selection of the vendor is to occur by the end of 2027. The solution is to perform live-firing in Exercise Talisman Saber in mid-2029, and an initial operational capability achieved in the early 2030s.
Importantly, the expeditionary air-defense system must integrate with radars from CEA Technologies and the Joint Air Battle Management System being developed by Lockheed Martin Australia.
Because of the time constraints, Canberra is pursuing direct commercial sale and U.S. Foreign Military Sales (FMS) avenues simultaneously.
The timing of the tender may boost the chances of non-American missile suppliers, as the U.S. grapples with depleted magazines after expending large amounts of missiles in its conflict with Iran.
A recent Congressional Research Service report warned , “Finite U.S. industrial base capacity introduces trade-offs between filling FMS orders and replenishing U.S. stockpiles. FMS delivery delays may result in cancellations, potentially affecting U.S. and partner interoperability and integration.”
Other options are available, however. For example, Australia could add AMRAAM-ER extended-range missiles to its existing NASAMS.
John Fry, managing director of Kongsberg Australia, told Defense News : “We’re definitely interested in that program. I think the great thing with the NASAMS architecture is Kongsberg and Raytheon are evolving that into full-spectrum air defense.”
Elsewhere, Lockheed Martin Australia fired an SM-2 missile from a trailer launcher in June, utilizing the Aegis combat system and a CEA radar. This demonstrated how a hybrid air defense system can make use of components already available in Australia.
About Gordon Arthur
Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

Rare 1964 Chevy Corvette Convertible L75 327/300 Rocks Gorgeous Saddle Tan, Has an Ace up Its Sleeve
31 photos
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales
This 1964 Chevrolet Corvette Convertible looks better than it did the day it rolled off the production line 62 years ago. It rocks the Saddle Tan gold finish over a matching Saddle Tan interior and a V8 engine, which makes it extremely rare.
General Motors produced a total of 22,229 Corvettes for the 1964 model year. Of them, 13,925 were convertibles, making up 62.6% of the total production run that year. And wait, the selection narrows even further.
Only 1,765 units across all engine types and body styles rolled off the production line in the rarest factory color offered for the 1964 lineup, Saddle Tan. Only 520 of them were convertibles. And this car right here is one of them.
Often described as gold, the official factory name for this iconic metallic shade was Saddle. Tan, Paint Code 932. It stands out as one of the most distinctive, period-correct color combinations of the C2 generation, highlighting the clean lines of the 1964 redesign.
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales This model year saw the removal of the previous year's faux hood vents and the addition of functional body ventilation on the driver's side, which meant a smoother overall silhouette. This car comes with NCRS Top Flight, which is the highest and most prestigious judging award presented by the National Corvette Restorers Society.
It is essentially the gold standard for Corvette restoration. To earn a Top Flight award, a Chevy Corvette must undergo a rigorous, highly detailed raw-point inspection process by a panel of NCRS master judges. The presence of the "NCRS" letters explain the asking price.
This car is pushed forward by the 327-cubic-inch V8 , with a single four-barrel carburetor. The V8 produces 300 horsepower (304 metric horsepower) and 360 pound-feet (488 Newton meters) of torque. A Muncie four-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure Corvette fashion, which makes it a pure driver’s car.
At the time, General Motors also offered the two-speed Powerglide automatic transmission. While the manual car was good for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.0 seconds and a top speed of 129 mph (208 kph), the automatic did 0 to 60 in 6.8 seconds and hit a top speed of 127 mph (204 kph).
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales Finding a 1964 Convertible in Saddle Tan over a matching tan interior is rare nowadays. Well-preserved, numbers-matching examples can go as far as $90,320, as indicated by classic.com. However, Vanguard Motors has listed this example for $169,900, which is nearly double the best-maintained cars out there. The price includes two convertible tops in body-matching color.
Back in 1964, the starting price for a C2 Chevy Corvette was exactly $4,037. The L75 327-cubic-inch V8 with 300 horsepower was a $53 option at the time. Meanwhile, the Saddle Tan Metallic paint was offered at no extra cost, since it was a standard factory choice that year.
